text:
Copenhagen is one of those rare destinations that feels different the moment you arrive.
It's clean.
It's calm.
And everything feels effortlessly elevated.
From colorful waterfront neighborhoods and storybook canals to cozy cafés, world-class dining, and iconic Scandinavian design, Copenhagen offers Europe at a slower, more intentional pace.
✅ Walkable, safe, and incredibly easy to explore
✅ Charming cafés and boutique hotels you will absolutely love
✅ A seamless blend of food, culture, history, and design
And the best part?
You can easily enhance the experience with:
✨ A quick trip across the Øresund Bridge to Sweden
✨ Incredible foodie experiences you will be talking about long after you return home
✨ A chance to embrace the famous Danish "hygge" lifestyle that's capturing travelers' attention worldwide
Copenhagen is ideal for:
❤️ Couples seeking a romantic European escape
🌍 Solo travelers looking for a safe and welcoming destination
✈️ Experienced travelers who have already visited Europe's major capitals and want something different
Advisor Tip: Copenhagen is an elegant, stress-free European experience. It's not about rushing from attraction to attraction. It's about slowing down, soaking in the atmosphere, and enjoying one of the most livable cities in the world.
This isn't just a vacation you take.
It's a destination you'll remember for years to come.

---

# Copenhagen, Denmark: Scandinavia's Perfect Gateway

## Why Copenhagen Captivates Travelers

Copenhagen is one of those rare cities that exceeds expectations. Its colorful harbor fronts, bicycle-filled streets, Michelin-starred restaurants, royal palaces, modern design districts, and laid-back atmosphere create an experience unlike any other European capital.

What surprises most visitors is how effortlessly everything works. Trains run on time, public transportation is efficient, English is spoken almost universally, and the city is exceptionally safe. Combined with Denmark's famous quality of life, Copenhagen serves as both a wonderful destination and an ideal home base for exploring Scandinavia.

---

# Denmark at a Glance

Denmark is the southernmost of the Scandinavian countries, consisting of the Jutland Peninsula and more than 400 islands. Despite its relatively small size, Denmark has exercised an outsized influence on world history, culture, science, architecture, and commerce.

The nation is home to approximately six million people and consistently ranks among the happiest countries in the world. Danish society places a strong emphasis on equality, trust, sustainability, education, and work/life balance.

The Danish people are often described as polite, pragmatic, environmentally conscious, and community-oriented. Visitors frequently notice the remarkable level of trust that exists within Danish society, where bicycles are often left unlocked and public spaces are meticulously maintained.

---

# A Brief History of Denmark

Denmark's history stretches back more than a thousand years.

The country rose to prominence during the Viking Age from approximately the eighth through eleventh centuries, when Danish Vikings explored, traded, and settled across much of Europe. Their influence reached England, Ireland, France, Iceland, Greenland, and even North America.

Denmark later became a major European kingdom and at one time ruled Norway and parts of Sweden. Over the centuries, it transitioned into a constitutional monarchy and developed into one of the world's most prosperous and stable democracies.

Today, Denmark successfully combines respect for its historical heritage with an embrace of innovation and sustainability.

---

# The Danish Concept of Hygge

No discussion of Denmark is complete without mentioning "hygge."

Pronounced roughly "hoo\-gah," hygge represents far more than simple coziness. It embodies warmth, comfort, meaningful connection, simplicity, and contentment.

Imagine:

• Candlelit cafés during winter. • Friends gathered around a dinner table. • Reading a book beside a fireplace. • Sharing pastries and coffee on a rainy afternoon.

Danes consider these moments essential rather than indulgent. Hygge is often cited as one reason Denmark performs so well in international happiness rankings.

Visitors quickly discover that hygge is not merely a marketing slogan. It is woven into everyday Danish life.

---

# Copenhagen's Culture

Copenhagen balances centuries-old traditions with contemporary creativity.

Highlights include:

• Royal palaces and historic castles. • Modern architectural masterpieces. • World-renowned design museums. • Vibrant waterfront neighborhoods. • Cutting-edge sustainable urban planning. • An active cycling culture.

The city hosts numerous festivals throughout the year celebrating jazz, food, film, literature, and the arts.

---

# Danish Cuisine

Denmark has quietly become one of the world's culinary powerhouses.

Traditional Danish dishes include:

• Smørrebrød (open\-faced sandwiches) • Frikadeller (Danish meatballs) • Stegt flæsk (crispy pork with potatoes) • Pickled herring • Danish pastries

Modern Danish cuisine has earned global recognition through New Nordic cooking, emphasizing locally sourced ingredients, seasonal produce, and culinary innovation.

Copenhagen boasts one of the highest concentrations of Michelin-starred restaurants in Europe.

Yet travelers can enjoy excellent meals at every budget level, from food halls to waterfront cafés.

---

# Education and Innovation

Denmark is widely admired for its education system.

Higher education is strongly supported, literacy rates are among the world's highest, and universities attract students from around the globe.

The country emphasizes critical thinking, collaboration, and creativity rather than memorization alone.

This educational focus has helped produce a highly skilled workforce and strong innovation economy.

---

# Denmark's Economy

Denmark maintains one of the strongest economies in Europe.

Major industries include:

• Pharmaceuticals • Renewable energy • Shipping and logistics • Biotechnology • Agriculture • Food production • Engineering • Information technology

The nation is particularly recognized as a global leader in wind energy and sustainable development.

---

# Art, Literature, and Music

## Literature

Denmark's most celebrated literary figure is Hans Christian Andersen, whose fairy tales such as The Little Mermaid, The Ugly Duckling, and The Emperor's New Clothes became global classics.

## Design and Art

Danish design is famous worldwide for its minimalist aesthetic, functional beauty, and timeless craftsmanship.

Furniture, architecture, lighting, and industrial design remain major Danish exports.

## Music

Denmark supports a thriving classical, jazz, pop, and electronic music scene. Copenhagen's annual jazz festival is among Europe's most respected music events.

---

# Five Famous Danish Contributions to Humanity

## 1. Hans Christian Andersen

The legendary author whose fairy tales have influenced generations around the world.

## 2. LEGO

Founded in Denmark in 1932, LEGO became one of the most iconic and beloved toy brands ever created.

## 3. Niels Bohr

One of the founders of modern quantum physics and a Nobel Prize-winning scientist.

## 4. The Øresund Bridge

A remarkable engineering achievement connecting Denmark and Sweden while transforming regional travel and commerce.

## 5. Wind Energy Leadership

Denmark helped pioneer modern commercial wind power and remains one of the world's leading renewable-energy innovators.

---

# Tourism in Denmark

Tourism represents an important component of Denmark's economy.

International visitors are drawn by:

• Copenhagen • Tivoli Gardens • Nyhavn Harbor • Viking heritage sites • Castles and palaces • Danish coastline • Cycling culture • Culinary experiences

Copenhagen has become one of Europe's premier city-break destinations and a frequent starting point for Scandinavian itineraries.

---

# Why Copenhagen Is the Ideal Base for Scandinavian Exploration

This may be Copenhagen's greatest advantage.

Within approximately:

• 20 minutes: Malmö, Sweden • 1 hour: Southern Sweden destinations • 5 hours: Stockholm by high\-speed rail • A few hours by air: Oslo, Bergen, Helsinki, Reykjavik, and countless Northern European destinations

The city sits at the crossroads of Scandinavia.

Travelers can enjoy Danish culture while easily taking day trips or multi-day excursions into Sweden and beyond.

This convenience is difficult to match elsewhere in Northern Europe.

---

# Best Time to Visit

## Best Overall

May through September

These months offer pleasant temperatures, extensive daylight, outdoor dining, canal cruises, and vibrant city life.

## Best Combination of Weather and Value

May and September

Many experienced travelers consider these shoulder-season months the sweet spot, offering fewer crowds, lower hotel prices, and excellent weather.

## Best for Christmas Atmosphere

Late November through December

Christmas markets, lights, and hygge create an unforgettable holiday experience.

---

# How Far in Advance Should You Book?

For May through September:

• Flights: 4 to 8 months ahead • Hotels: 3 to 6 months ahead

For Christmas and major summer festivals:

• 6 to 10 months ahead is preferable.

For winter travel outside holiday periods:

• 2 to 4 months is usually sufficient.

---

# Approximate Cost of a One-Week Copenhagen Vacation

## Solo Traveler

Flights: $800–$1,500

Hotel: $900–$2,100

Food: $300–$700

Attractions & Local Transport: $150–$350

Estimated Total: $2,150–$4,650

---

## Couple

Flights: $1,600–$3,000

Hotel: $1,300–$3,000

Food: $800–$1,400

Attractions & Transport: $300–$600

Estimated Total: $4,000–$8,000

Travel styles can significantly impact these numbers, but they represent realistic mid-market estimates.

---

# Approximate Nonstop Airfare from the Continental United States

Roundtrip Per Person

Economy: $700–$1,300

Premium Economy: $1,400–$2,500

Business Class: $2,800–$6,500+

First Class (when available): $5,000–$12,000+

Departure city, season, airline, and booking window can significantly influence pricing.

---

# Final Thoughts

Copenhagen succeeds where many major cities struggle. It balances history with innovation, elegance with accessibility, and sophistication with genuine warmth.

Visitors can spend mornings touring royal palaces, afternoons cycling along the waterfront, evenings dining at world-class restaurants, and the next day be exploring Sweden.

Whether you are visiting Scandinavia for the first time or returning for another adventure, Copenhagen offers one of Europe's most enjoyable and strategically located urban experiences. Few cities provide such a perfect combination of culture, convenience, safety, beauty, and quality of life.

For travelers dreaming of Scandinavia, Copenhagen is not simply a destination. It is the ideal starting point for discovering an entire region.

---

CURRENT HEADLINES 🛰️

Saturday, November 14, 2026
Reporting cutoff: Approximately 6:21 p.m. EST.

─────────────── ★ ───────────────

Domestic U.S. ⋆ International Affairs ⋆ Business & Markets ⋆ Science & Health ⋆ National Security ⋆ Military Developments ⋆ Other Notable Stories ⋆ America First Read.

─────────────── ★ ───────────────

“In a time of universal deceit, telling the truth is a revolutionary act.” ~ Commonly attributed to George Orwell.

─────────────── ★ ───────────────

This digest covers consequential U.S. and world developments from a conservative and center-right vantage. Stories are organized by significance, with allegations, official announcements, and unconfirmed claims identified where appropriate. Analysis is confined to the America First Read.

─────────────── ★ ───────────────

ESTIMATED TOTAL READING TIME: 18–22 minutes

─────────────── ★ ───────────────

DOMESTIC U.S. NEWS 🦅

FAA investigates contractor equipment failure as nationwide flight disruption continues

The Federal Aviation Administration continued investigating the telecommunications and radar problems that forced a nationwide ground stop Friday, creating one of the most significant disruptions to American air travel in decades.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the failure involved problems associated with replacing aging copper wiring with fiber-optic equipment. Investigators are examining whether a faulty router installed by contractor L3Harris or an installation-related problem contributed to the system overload.

Airlines canceled thousands of additional flights Saturday as they attempted to reposition aircraft and crews. More than 6,000 cancellations were reported, with thousands of additional delays. The FAA expects operations to return to normal by Sunday.

Duffy warned that the incident demonstrates the urgent need to modernize America's aging air-traffic-control infrastructure and renewed his call for approximately $50 billion in modernization funding.

Source: Fox News; New York Post; Reuters; Associated Press; U.S. Department of Transportation.
AP News+3

FBI investigates bomb discovered at Illinois ethanol facility

Federal and local authorities investigated a powerful explosive device discovered at BioUrja Renewables, an ethanol facility in Peoria, Illinois.

The discovery prompted evacuation orders for residents and workers within approximately one mile of the facility because of the device's potential blast radius. Thousands of people were affected, and emergency shelters were established.

Bomb technicians rendered the device safe Friday evening. Authorities continued investigating the facility and surrounding area, while the FBI and other law-enforcement agencies examined the circumstances surrounding the threat.

No injuries were reported. Officials had not publicly identified a suspect or established a motive.

Source: Fox News; Washington Post; Associated Press; CNN.
The Washington Post+2

Democrat flips Alaska governor's mansion after Republican infighting

Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins won Alaska's gubernatorial election, defeating Trump-endorsed Republican Bernadette Wilson under the state's ranked-choice voting system.

Kreiss-Tomkins, a former state legislator, becomes Alaska's first Democratic governor since 1998. The Associated Press called the race Friday evening.

The contest featured Republican divisions and competing political interests, complicating the GOP's effort to retain the governor's mansion. Kreiss-Tomkins campaigned on affordability, public education, and increased taxation of oil and gas producers.

The result adds another significant Democratic victory to the party's gains in the 2026 midterm elections.

Source: Fox News; CBS News; Associated Press.
Fox News+1

Van Hollen intensifies challenge to Schumer for Senate Democratic leadership

Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) intensified his campaign to replace Sen. Chuck Schumer as Democratic Senate leader, arguing that the party needs new leadership following its midterm victories.

Van Hollen launched a campaign-style website and began publicly criticizing what he considers the party's overly cautious political approach.

Although he has attracted support from several incoming Democratic senators and progressive figures, Schumer continues to hold a substantial advantage among sitting Democratic lawmakers.

The contest reflects a broader struggle over the party's direction as Democrats prepare to assume greater congressional power in January.

Source: Fox News; Washington Post; Washington Examiner.
The Washington Post+2

─────────────── ★ ───────────────

INTERNATIONAL AFFAIRS 🌐

Trump considers restraint as Iran blockade continues

President Trump has reportedly told senior advisers that he may hold off on additional attacks against Iran unless Tehran or its Houthi allies undertake further provocations.

According to Reuters, the president has not settled on a final strategy for ending the conflict. The administration continues to maintain economic and military pressure, while American forces remain prepared to escalate if necessary.

The U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports began Saturday morning. Washington is seeking to restrict Iranian maritime commerce and prevent unauthorized passage through the Strait of Hormuz.

Trump's position reflects a potential preference for maintaining economic and strategic pressure rather than immediately expanding military operations. However, the administration has not ruled out additional strikes.

Source: Fox News; Reuters; New York Post; The Epoch Times.
Investing.com+1

Trump, Xi, and Putin prepare for unprecedented trilateral summit

The White House and Kremlin confirmed plans for President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin to meet Thursday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China.

The proposed gathering would bring together the leaders of the world's three largest nuclear powers for an unprecedented joint meeting.

Trump intends to discuss the Iran conflict and his interest in negotiating a new nuclear-arms agreement that would include China. The previous U.S.-Russian nuclear arms treaty expired in February, removing longstanding restrictions on the two countries' strategic arsenals.

No major agreements are expected from the meeting. Nevertheless, the gathering carries considerable diplomatic significance, particularly as Russia continues its war against Ukraine and maintains close strategic ties with Beijing.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has expressed concern about discussions concerning Ukraine taking place without Kyiv's participation.

Source: Associated Press; Washington Post; Reuters; Washington Examiner.
AP News+2

Ecuadorian fishermen prepare lawsuit challenging U.S. military boat strikes

Sixteen Ecuadorian fishermen who survived a U.S. military attack on their vessel are preparing to sue the Trump administration over the March incident.

The fishermen allege that their boat was struck by armed drones in the eastern Pacific despite having no connection to drug trafficking. Two crew members reportedly suffered serious burns, and the vessel was destroyed.

The plaintiffs further allege that survivors were detained and mistreated after the attack. Their lawsuit challenges the legality of the military operation and seeks financial compensation.

The Defense Department declined to comment on pending litigation. The allegations have not been adjudicated.

The case raises significant questions about the legal authority governing American military operations against suspected drug-trafficking vessels and the administration's broader counter-narcotics campaign.

Source: The Guardian; Associated Press.
The Guardian

─────────────── ★ ───────────────

BUSINESS & MARKETS 💹

Nvidia turmoil weighs on technology shares and investor confidence

Nvidia remained under pressure following the reported resignation of founder Jensen Huang as CEO, president, and board member. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress was named interim CEO while the company searches for permanent leadership.

The controversy follows scrutiny of Huang's relationship with a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspect of having connections to Beijing. Those allegations have not been independently established.

The company's independent directors have retained outside legal counsel to investigate the matter.

The uncertainty has contributed to a broader technology-sector selloff, with semiconductor manufacturers and artificial-intelligence-related companies experiencing significant declines.

Nvidia's situation carries implications beyond its stock price. The company occupies a central position in America's artificial-intelligence industry and its competition with China.

Source: Fox News; Reuters; The Wall Street Journal; Washington Examiner.
Business Recorder+2

Wholesale inflation remains elevated despite modest monthly increase

The Labor Department's October Producer Price Index showed a 0.3% monthly increase, following a revised 1.4% increase in September.

On an annual basis, producer prices increased 6.5%, the largest 12-month advance since November 2022.

Goods prices rose 0.5%, while services increased 0.2%. Transportation costs also showed renewed pressure.

Although the monthly increase was smaller than September's, the annual figures suggest that inflation remains a significant concern for American businesses and consumers.

The numbers also complicate the Federal Reserve's efforts to determine whether monetary policy should remain restrictive.

Source: Reuters; Fox News; U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics; Associated Press.
Kiplinger+1

Wall Street retreats as technology stocks face renewed selling pressure

U.S. stock markets declined Friday as investor concerns surrounding Nvidia and the artificial-intelligence sector weighed on technology shares.

The Nasdaq Composite fell approximately 0.9%, while the S&P 500 declined 0.4%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average edged up approximately 0.1%.

Semiconductor stocks experienced particularly heavy selling, with AMD and Broadcom among the companies suffering significant losses.

Despite Friday's declines, the major indexes finished the week with overall gains.

Investors are now looking toward Nvidia's upcoming earnings report and further inflation data for indications of the technology sector's direction and the Federal Reserve's next move.

Source: Reuters; Kiplinger; Business Recorder.
Kiplinger+1

─────────────── ★ ───────────────

SCIENCE & HEALTH ⚕️

United States loses measles elimination status after sustained transmission

The United States has reportedly lost its measles-elimination status after the Pan American Health Organization determined that the virus has become reestablished through sustained domestic transmission.

The country first achieved measles elimination status in 2000, following decades of vaccination efforts.

More than 5,400 measles cases have been reported in 2026, exceeding the previous year's total. The resurgence has been particularly severe in Pennsylvania, while additional outbreaks have affected multiple states.

The determination reflects the continued circulation of the same virus strain for at least 12 months. The Pan American Health Organization's public announcement is expected November 17.

Public-health experts have pointed to declining vaccination rates and gaps in community immunity as contributing factors.

The development represents a major setback for American public health and underscores the importance of maintaining vaccination coverage and effective disease surveillance.

Source: Fox News; CBS News; Reuters; KFF Health News; Associated Press.
KFF Health News+3

─────────────── ★ ───────────────

NATIONAL SECURITY 🛡️

Ecuadorian lawsuit challenges legal authority behind U.S. anti-narcotics strikes

The lawsuit being prepared by Ecuadorian fishermen against the Trump administration has broader implications for American national-security policy.

The plaintiffs challenge the administration's authority to use military force against suspected drug-trafficking vessels outside an established armed conflict.

The Trump administration has defended its broader campaign against narcotics networks and organizations it identifies as narco-terrorist threats.

The case could bring renewed scrutiny to the legal standards governing maritime interdictions, intelligence assessments, targeting decisions, and the treatment of survivors.

The administration's position and the plaintiffs' allegations will ultimately be tested through the legal process.

Source: The Guardian; U.S. Southern Command statements as reported.
The Guardian

─────────────── ★ ───────────────

MILITARY DEVELOPMENTS  🪖

U.S. blockade of Iranian ports takes effect as Hormuz tensions escalate

The U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports took effect Saturday at 10 a.m. Eastern Time, following the administration's announcement that American forces would intercept vessels violating the restrictions.

The operation represents a significant escalation in Washington's economic and maritime pressure campaign against Tehran.

The United States is also seeking to address the threat posed by Iranian naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic waterway through which a substantial portion of the world's oil shipments normally passes.

Britain and Spain have declined to participate in the American blockade. France and Britain have instead proposed discussions about a separate defensive multinational maritime mission intended to protect shipping.

The disagreement illustrates divisions among Western allies over how to respond to Iran without widening the conflict.

Source: Reuters; Associated Press; Council on Foreign Relations; Fox News.
Council on Foreign Relations+2

Iran claims three oil tankers struck naval mines in Strait of Hormuz

Iranian naval authorities claimed Saturday that three oil tankers caught fire after striking naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz.

Iranian state media reported that one vessel struck a mine in the eastern portion of the strait during the morning, while two additional vessels reportedly struck mines later in the day.

The Revolutionary Guards Navy alleged that the latter vessels were attempting to use a prohibited route.

Reuters reported that it could not independently verify the claims.

The reports underscore the danger facing international shipping as Washington and Tehran compete for control over maritime access. The potential disruption to commercial shipping and energy supplies remains a major concern for international markets.

Source: Reuters; Iranian state media as reported by Reuters.
Reuters

Trump weighs military options while American forces maintain readiness

Although President Trump has reportedly considered holding off on further attacks against Iran, American military planners continue preparing for possible escalation.

Reuters reported that a third aircraft carrier was expected to move into the Middle East in the coming days to replace one of the two currently operating in the region. Officials have not ruled out the possibility that all three could remain available if circumstances require.

The administration continues to evaluate military options while assessing weapons inventories, regional threats, and the strategic consequences of renewed attacks.

The situation places considerable importance on deterrence, force readiness, and the administration's ability to preserve American leverage without exhausting resources needed elsewhere.

Source: Reuters; Fox News.
https://t.co/z26JVrBos2

─────────────── ★ ───────────────

OTHER NOTABLE AND UNUSUAL STORIES 🌀

FAA disruption forces college basketball postponement

The nationwide aviation shutdown affected college athletics as well as commercial travelers.

Cornell University's scheduled men's basketball game against UNC Greensboro was postponed after the visiting team encountered travel difficulties associated with the aviation disruption.

The incident illustrates how an infrastructure failure affecting one sector can produce consequences throughout the broader economy and public life.

Source: New York Post; Associated Press.
New York Post+1

California's Mavericks Beach braces for enormous waves

California's famous Mavericks surf break is expected to experience exceptionally large waves, potentially reaching approximately 50 feet.

The forecast has drawn attention from the big-wave surfing community, where conditions at Mavericks can create some of the most dangerous and demanding surfing opportunities in the world.

Large-wave conditions also raise concerns about ocean safety, rescue operations, and hazardous coastal conditions.

Source: Washington Post.
The Washington Post

─────────────── ★ ───────────────

AMERICA FIRST READ 🇺🇸

Analysis, not reporting.

Saturday's developments reinforce several central themes of the America First agenda: national sovereignty, military deterrence, economic security, technological independence, and the importance of competent domestic institutions.

Iran and the strategic value of American leverage

The administration's decision to maintain its blockade while considering restraint from additional strikes presents an important test of American foreign policy.

Military superiority is a source of leverage, but the ability to exercise that leverage intelligently is equally important.

The Strait of Hormuz is a critical international shipping corridor. Any sustained disruption carries consequences for energy markets, international commerce, and American consumers.

The reported tanker incidents, if confirmed, demonstrate the potential danger of allowing Iran to exercise unchecked control over maritime passage.

The administration must maintain a clear distinction between applying pressure and becoming trapped in an open-ended regional conflict. Protecting American personnel, preventing Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons, and preserving freedom of navigation are legitimate strategic objectives. Achieving them without committing the United States to another prolonged war should remain a priority.

The coming summit and America's position among the great powers

The planned meeting between Trump, Xi, and Putin could become one of the most consequential diplomatic gatherings of the year.

Bringing the leaders of the world's three largest nuclear powers together creates an opportunity to discuss strategic arms control, the Iran conflict, and the future of international security.

However, symbolism should not be mistaken for achievement.

China and Russia have developed increasingly close economic, military, and diplomatic relationships. Beijing has also become an important supplier of technology and economic support to Moscow.

Washington must approach the meeting with a clear understanding of American interests. Any arms-control agreement must protect U.S. security rather than simply produce a diplomatic announcement.

Ukraine's absence from discussions concerning its own future would also be a serious consideration. American diplomacy should not create the impression that the sovereignty of an ally can be negotiated away without its participation.

Economic stability remains an unfinished assignment

The latest producer-price figures demonstrate that inflation remains a serious concern.

A modest monthly increase is encouraging only if it becomes part of a sustained downward trend. American families continue to judge economic performance through grocery bills, housing costs, energy prices, insurance, and everyday expenses.

The administration's efforts to reduce shipping costs and maintain energy security are relevant to that objective.

But the ultimate measure of economic success is whether Americans experience meaningful improvements in purchasing power and living standards.

Technological independence and national security

The Nvidia controversy illustrates the growing connection between corporate leadership, advanced technology, and national security.

Artificial intelligence and semiconductor manufacturing are now central components of America's economic and military competitiveness.

The United States cannot afford to become dependent on foreign adversaries for critical technologies or allow inadequate corporate oversight to compromise strategic advantages.

The allegations surrounding Nvidia remain unproven, but the broader issue deserves serious attention.

Protecting intellectual property, maintaining effective export controls, and encouraging domestic technological innovation should remain national priorities.

Public safety and government accountability

The FAA disruption is another reminder that America's infrastructure requires serious attention.

The nation cannot maintain global leadership while relying on aging systems that are vulnerable to failures capable of disrupting thousands of flights.

Modernization must be accompanied by competent management, effective oversight, and clear accountability.

The Peoria bomb investigation offers a different reminder of the importance of law enforcement and emergency preparedness. Public safety depends on institutions capable of identifying threats and responding effectively.

The political consequences of the midterms

Democratic victories in Alaska and elsewhere demonstrate the political challenges facing Republicans after the midterm elections.

Republicans must recognize that political loyalty alone does not guarantee continued public support.

Economic performance, effective leadership, and the ability to deliver tangible improvements in everyday life will determine whether the party can rebuild its coalition.

The administration's America First agenda ultimately rests on results: secure borders, affordable energy, strong national defense, technological leadership, reliable infrastructure, and a foreign policy that places American interests first.

The challenge is translating those priorities into lasting accomplishments rather than allowing political rhetoric to become an end in itself.

─────────────── ★ ───────────────

COVERAGE & VERIFICATION NOTE

This digest reflects reporting available through Saturday, November 14, 2026, at approximately 6:21 p.m. Eastern Time.

Coverage draws on conservative and center-right reporting, including:

Fox News ⋆ New York Post ⋆ Washington Examiner ⋆ The Epoch Times ⋆ Newsmax ⋆ The Daily Wire

Additional verification and reporting were drawn from Reuters, Associated Press, CBS News, KFF Health News, the Washington Post, and other identified sources.

Important verification distinctions:

The Iranian claims concerning three tankers striking naval mines have not been independently verified.
Allegations concerning Nvidia's former CEO and possible Chinese intelligence connections remain under investigation and should not be treated as established findings.

The Ecuadorian fishermen's allegations are claims made in anticipated litigation, not judicial findings.

The measles-elimination decision was reported by health organizations with knowledge of the PAHO determination; a formal public announcement was expected November 17.

The FAA investigation into the equipment failure remains ongoing. Responsibility has not yet been conclusively established.

Quotation verification: The opening quotation is commonly attributed to George Orwell, but the Orwell Society explicitly states that he did not say it. Quote Investigator likewise found no substantive evidence that the quotation originated with Orwell. The attribution is therefore qualified rather than presented as authenticated.

text:
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

This has been a wild year for AI. If you’ve spent much time online, you’ve probably bumped into images generated by AI systems like DALL-E 2 or Stable Diffusion, or jokes, essays, or other text written by ChatGPT, the latest incarnation of OpenAI’s large language model GPT-3.

Sometimes it’s obvious when a picture or a piece of text has been created by an AI. But increasingly, the output these models generate can easily fool us into thinking it was made by a human. And large language models in particular are confident bullshitters: they create text that sounds correct but in fact may be full of falsehoods. 

While that doesn’t matter if it’s just a bit of fun, it can have serious consequences if AI models are used to offer unfiltered health advice or provide other forms of important information. AI systems could also make it stupidly easy to produce reams of misinformation, abuse, and spam, distorting the information we consume and even our sense of reality. It could be particularly worrying around elections, for example. 

The proliferation of these easily accessible large language models raises an important question: How will we know whether what we read online is written by a human or a machine? I’ve just published a story looking into the tools we currently have to spot AI-generated text. Spoiler alert: Today’s detection tool kit is woefully inadequate against ChatGPT. 

But there is a more serious long-term implication. We may be witnessing, in real time, the birth of a snowball of bullshit. 

Large language models are trained on data sets that are built by scraping the internet for text, including all the toxic, silly, false, malicious things humans have written online. The finished AI models regurgitate these falsehoods as fact, and their output is spread everywhere online. Tech companies scrape the internet again, scooping up AI-written text that they use to train bigger, more convincing models, which humans can use to generate even more nonsense before it is scraped again and again, ad nauseam.

This problem—AI feeding on itself and producing increasingly polluted output—extends to images. “The internet is now forever contaminated with images made by AI,” Mike Cook, an AI researcher at King’s College London, told my colleague Will Douglas Heaven in his new piece on the future of generative AI models. 

“The images that we made in 2022 will be a part of any model that is made from now on.”

In the future, it’s going to get trickier and trickier to find good-quality, guaranteed AI-free training data, says Daphne Ippolito, a senior research scientist at Google Brain, the company’s research unit for deep learning. It’s not going to be good enough to just blindly hoover text up from the internet anymore, if we want to keep future AI models from having biases and falsehoods embedded to the nth degree.

“It’s really important to consider whether we need to be training on the entirety of the internet or whether there’s ways we can just filter the things that are high quality and are going to give us the kind of language model we want,” says Ippolito. 

Building tools for detecting AI-generated text will become crucial when people inevitably try to submit AI-written scientific papers or academic articles, or use AI to create fake news or misinformation. 

Technical tools can help, but humans also need to get savvier.

Ippolito says there are a few telltale signs of AI-generated text. Humans are messy writers. Our text is full of typos and slang, and looking out for these sorts of mistakes and subtle nuances is a good way to identify text written by a human. In contrast, large language models work by predicting the next word in a sentence, and they are more likely to use common words like “the,” “it,” or “is” instead of wonky, rare words. And while they almost never misspell words, they do get things wrong. Ippolito says people should look out for subtle inconsistencies or factual errors in texts that are presented as fact, for example. 

The good news:her research shows that with practice, humans can train ourselves to better spot AI-generated text. Maybe there is hope for us all yet. 

Deeper Learning

A Roomba recorded a woman on the toilet. How did screenshots end up on Facebook?

This story made my skin crawl. Earlier this year my colleague Eileen Guo got hold of 15 screenshots of private photos taken by a robot vacuum, including images of someone sitting on the toilet, posted to closed social media groups. 

Who is watching? iRobot, the developer of the Roomba robot vacuum, says that the images did not come from the homes of customers but “paid collectors and employees” who signed written agreements acknowledging that they were sending data streams, including video, back to the company for training purposes. But it’s not clear whether these people knew that humans, in particular, would be viewing these images in order to train the AI. 

Why this matters: The story illustrates the growing practice of sharing potentially sensitive data to train algorithms, as well as the surprising, globe-spanning journey that a single image can take—in this case, from homes in North America, Europe, and Asia to the servers of Massachusetts-based iRobot, from there to San Francisco–based Scale AI, and finally to Scale’s contracted data workers around the world. Together, the images reveal a whole data supply chain—and new points where personal information could leak out—that few consumers are even aware of. Read the story here.

Bits and Bytes

OpenAI founder Sam Altman tells us what he learned from DALL-E 2 
Altman tells Will Douglas Heaven why he thinks DALLE-2 was such a big hit, what lessons he learned from its success, and what models like it mean for society. (MIT Technology Review) 

Artists can now opt out of the next version of Stable Diffusion
The decision follows a heated public debate between artists and tech companies over how text-to-image AI models should be trained. Since the launch of Stable Diffusion, artists have been up in arms, arguing that the model rips them off by including many of their copyrighted works without any payment or attribution. (MIT Technology Review) 

China has banned lots of types of deepfakes 
The Chinese Cyberspace Administration has banned deepfakes that are created without their subject’s permission and that go against socialist values or disseminate “Illegal and harmful information.” (The Register) 

What it’s like to be a chatbot’s human backup
As a student, writer Laura Preston had an unusual job: stepping in when a real estate AI chatbot called Brenda went off-script. The goal was that customers would not notice. The story shows just how dumb the AI of today can be in real-life situations, and how much human work goes into maintaining the illusion of intelligent machines. (The Guardian)

Washington State 

Biofuel Development Opportunity (BDO) Zone for 'Woody Biomass'

LEWIS COUNTY 

Lewis County, Washington Named North America’s First Insurable BDO Zone, Bringing Insurance-Backed Feedstock Cost Certainty to Biomass Investment

Nov. 14, 2026

Ecostrat, New Energy Risk and the Economic Alliance of Lewis County today announced that the Lewis County, Washington BDO Zone for Woody Biomass has been designated the first Insurable BDO Zone. The Zone's 'AA' Rating has been upgraded to 'AA Insurable' following a preliminary finding by New Energy Risk that the Zone meets its initial underwriting pre-screening criteria for Feedstock Supply Insurance™ (FSI).

"Investors evaluating Lewis County consistently ask two questions: is the fiber available, and what will it cost over the life of a facility," said Todd Chaput, Executive Director, Economic Alliance of Lewis County. 
"Our BDO Zone rating answered the first. This designation answers the second and gives Lewis County a site-selection advantage no other region can offer today."

"Feedstock risk has long been the point at which promising biomass projects stall," said Jordan Solomon, President of Ecostrat and Chairman of the BDO Zone Initiative. "By pairing a BDO Zone Rating with insurance prequalification, an Insurable BDO Zone puts another powerful tool in the toolbox for local economic developers. Lewis County is the first, and we expect it to set the standard for regions across North America."

"NER is committed to supporting the growth of the bioeconomy and Ecostrat and the Economic Alliance of Lewis County share this vision," said George Schulz, CEO of New Energy Risk. "The BDO Zone Initiative demonstrates Ecostrat's keen insight to woodwaste value streams that enables access to feedstock supply insurance that will further the success of biofuel project development."

10. From the Hoover Dam to the Microchip: The Industrial World Becomes the Digital World
In September 1935, President Franklin D. Roosevelt dedicated the Hoover Dam.
Its massive concrete structure rose from the Colorado River between Nevada and Arizona.
The dam was an engineering triumph of the American industrial era.
Concrete placement was completed in May 1935, major associated works continued into 1936, and the first generator began full operation that October.
The project supported electricity generation, water storage and regional development.
But the dam was also shaped by human costs, including dangerous working conditions, environmental transformation and discriminatory employment practices documented in federal historical records.
Once again, great engineering raised difficult questions about whose interests the project served.
The dam represented an era when technological power was expressed through enormous physical structures.
Then, in November 1971, a much smaller device appeared.
It contained roughly 2,300 transistors.
Its name was the Intel 4004.
And it helped launch the modern microprocessor industry.
There is an extraordinary human story behind this chip.
The project began because the Japanese company Busicom wanted specialized electronics for a calculator.
Intel engineers proposed a more flexible architecture.
Ted Hoff, Stan Mazor and Federico Faggin contributed essential elements of the design, while Busicom engineer Masatoshi Shima played an important role in its development.
The resulting chip could be programmed for multiple tasks rather than built for one narrow function.
Intel ultimately secured rights to market the technology more broadly.
A project intended to improve a calculator helped transform computing.
The 4004 was not the first electronic computer, nor did it emerge independently of earlier semiconductor research.
Its significance was the commercial realization of a general-purpose central processing unit on a single chip.
The lesson is almost comically appropriate.
A Japanese company wanted a better calculator.
An American semiconductor company saw a broader opportunity.
Together, their engineers helped create a foundation for the digital age.
History rarely follows the tidy boundaries of national mythology.
From the 4004 came generations of increasingly sophisticated processors.
Computers moved from specialized institutions into offices, homes, vehicles and pockets.
The technology underlying modern artificial intelligence grew from this wider accumulation of semiconductor engineering, algorithms, software and global manufacturing capacity.
Today, the smallest objects can contain more computational power than earlier generations could imagine.
But computational power is not the same thing as wisdom.
A machine may process millions of instructions without knowing whether its objective is morally defensible.
The old Promethean problem has returned in silicon.

11. The Century That Proved Technology Does Not Make Us Moral
The twentieth century delivered astonishing improvements in medicine, transportation, communications and productivity.
It also witnessed two world wars, industrialized genocide and the development of nuclear weapons.
Scientific knowledge made antibiotics, vaccines and modern medical technologies possible.
It also made chemical warfare and nuclear destruction possible.
Industrial organization could mass-produce affordable consumer goods.
It could also mass-produce weapons.
Railways could carry families across continents.
They could also transport prisoners to concentration camps.
The same scientific principles that helped humanity understand atomic structure made nuclear reactors and atomic bombs possible.
Technology amplifies human capability.
It does not independently determine how that capability will be used.
This distinction matters because modern accounts of progress often confuse three different achievements:
We can do more.
We can produce more.
We have become better.
The first two statements can be measured through energy consumption, industrial output or computing capacity.
The third requires moral judgment.
There is no automatic equation linking technological advancement to ethical progress.
Yet rejecting technological progress would also ignore extraordinary improvements in human well-being.
According to historical estimates compiled by Our World in Data, global average life expectancy rose from approximately 32 years in 1900 to about 73 years in 2023.
The improvement reflects many factors, including public sanitation, nutrition, vaccination, medical advances and rising living standards.
No single nation or civilization deserves exclusive credit.
Scientific knowledge and public-health practices developed through international cooperation and were adapted by societies worldwide.
The achievement belongs to humanity.
But so does the responsibility for what comes next.

12. The Environmental Bill Is Arriving
For generations, industrial societies treated the atmosphere as an almost unlimited dumping ground.
Coal powered factories and railways.
Oil powered automobiles and aircraft.
Natural gas heated homes and generated electricity.
The resulting energy abundance transformed human civilization.
But burning fossil fuels also released enormous quantities of carbon dioxide.
Before industrialization, atmospheric carbon dioxide concentration was approximately 280 parts per million.
According to the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, the global monthly mean reached approximately 426 parts per million in July 2026.
The consequences include global warming, changing precipitation patterns, increasing heat extremes and other risks documented by climate science.
This creates a profound irony.
The same scientific civilization that developed the machinery responsible for much of the emissions also developed the instruments, mathematical models and observational systems that reveal the danger.
Scientists can now detect atmospheric changes invisible to earlier generations.
The problem is no longer simply ignorance.
It is the difficulty of coordinating political and economic action when benefits and costs are distributed unequally across countries, industries and generations.
Some critics argue that Western industrialization created a model of consumption that the planet cannot sustain.
Others emphasize that technological innovation—including renewable energy, storage, efficient infrastructure and advanced nuclear technologies—offers pathways to higher living standards with lower emissions.
Both concerns deserve serious consideration.
Energy poverty is real.
Environmental limits are real.
A credible future must address both.
The historical challenge has changed.
The nineteenth century asked how to produce enormous quantities of energy.
The twenty-first century asks how to produce and use energy without undermining the environmental systems on which civilization depends.

13. In 2026, the West Faces a New Paradox: More Intelligence, Less Political Confidence
Two developments reveal the tension particularly clearly.
The first concerns innovation.
In 2025, the Economics Prize recognized scholars explaining how technological change can support sustained economic growth.
The second concerns democracy.
In March 2026, Freedom House released its annual assessment of political rights and civil liberties.
It reported that global freedom had declined for the twentieth consecutive year in 2025.
According to its methodology, 54 countries experienced deterioration while 35 registered improvements.
Only about 21 percent of the world's population lived in countries classified as Free.
The report also identified significant deterioration in the United States, although it noted the continued resilience of many established democracies.
Another research organization, the V-Dem Institute, reached similarly worrying conclusions in its 2026 Democracy Report.
Such indices use different definitions and measurement methods. Their ratings are informed assessments, not unquestionable verdicts accepted by every political scientist.
Nevertheless, the broader concern is difficult to dismiss.
Many societies possess more technological capability than ever before while struggling with declining trust, polarization, misinformation and pressure on political institutions.
Meanwhile, artificial intelligence is reopening an ancient debate about how knowledge should be governed.
The European Union's AI Act and its 2026 amendments demonstrate one response: regulating particular risks while attempting to preserve innovation.
Other policymakers and companies argue that excessive regulation may slow development, reduce competition or discourage valuable experimentation.
Supporters of stronger safeguards point to surveillance, discrimination, fraud, manipulation and the concentration of technological power.
This debate is not simply Europe versus America, or the West versus China.
Artificial intelligence has become a global undertaking involving scientific institutions, researchers, industrial supply chains and governments across many regions.
The real questions are broader.
Who controls the systems?
Who benefits from their productivity?
Who bears the risks?
Who can challenge a decision made by a powerful institution—or by software acting on its behalf?
The historical struggle between knowledge and authority has acquired a new form.
The question Euclid helped make intellectually respectable—Can you demonstrate that your claim is justified?—is becoming equally relevant to powerful computational systems.

14. Did Western Civilization Create Modernity—or Simply Benefit From Historical Luck?
Historians disagree, and the disagreement matters.
One interpretation credits distinctive Western institutions.
It points to scientific societies, commercial competition, property rights, representative institutions and a culture that eventually rewarded innovation.
From this perspective, Europe's rise was not inevitable, but its intellectual and institutional evolution helped create unusually favourable conditions for sustained progress.
A second interpretation emphasizes historical contingency.
Accessible coal deposits, colonial resources, military advantage, geographic connections and favourable trade conditions all contributed to Europe's rise.
Supporters of this view argue that describing the outcome as evidence of cultural superiority confuses historical success with inevitable destiny.
A third approach combines these explanations.
Institutions mattered, but they evolved within material circumstances.
Scientific ideas mattered, but they moved across cultural borders.
Colonial exploitation mattered, but it cannot by itself explain every breakthrough in engineering or productivity.
The debate becomes less illuminating when participants insist on two extreme conclusions.
One is that Western civilization alone created everything valuable in modern life.
The other is that Western civilization contributed nothing distinctive and achieved its global position solely through conquest.
Neither adequately explains the historical record.
European scientific institutions helped create exceptionally productive systems of research and innovation.
But those systems drew on knowledge from many civilizations.
European imperial powers inflicted enormous harm.
But their societies also produced and contested principles that later contributed to expanding political and legal equality.
The same civilization could defend liberty abroad while denying it at home.
And the victims of exclusion could appeal to its proclaimed ideals in order to demand change.
This tension is not a minor footnote.
It is central to understanding how modern political and moral progress has occurred.
The most useful historical lesson may therefore be neither civilizational pride nor civilizational shame.
It is the recognition that achievement and responsibility must be examined together.

15. What This History Means for Your Career, Your Money and Your Children
It is tempting to treat ancient Greece, the Renaissance and the Industrial Revolution as subjects for museums and university classrooms.
But their underlying lessons remain unexpectedly practical.
Consider education.
Euclid's intellectual legacy reminds us that memorizing an answer is less valuable than understanding why it is correct.
A student trained to examine evidence, identify assumptions and question errors possesses a skill that remains useful even when specific technologies become obsolete.
Consider entrepreneurship.
The Intel 4004 illustrates how a narrowly defined commercial problem can lead to an entirely new market.
The breakthrough did not begin with a grand announcement about changing civilization.
It began with a customer who needed a calculator.
The lesson is not that every small idea will become revolutionary.
It is that useful innovation often emerges when people reconsider the structure of a familiar problem.
Consider investing.
The Industrial Revolution and the semiconductor era demonstrate that transformative technologies create enormous economic opportunities.
But identifying a great technology is not the same as identifying a good investment.
Companies fail.
Industries become competitive.
Promising innovations can arrive too early, prove too expensive or generate benefits that competitors capture.
Creative destruction rewards some investors while punishing others.
Consider politics.
The development of constitutional institutions reminds us that no political leader, corporation or ideology should be trusted without accountability.
Institutions that permit criticism, correction and peaceful succession may be less glamorous than charismatic leadership.
They are also essential safeguards against human error.
Consider family life.
Scientific progress has improved survival and health, but technology cannot replace every human good.
A parent can provide a child with sophisticated devices, instant information and remarkable educational tools.
Still, curiosity, kindness, discipline, judgment and the capacity to cooperate remain fundamental.
A civilization's future depends partly on what each generation teaches the next.
The most enduring inheritance is not a particular machine.
It is the ability to learn, question, build and accept responsibility.

16. The Final Frontier: Can Humanity Become a Civilization of the Stars?
The original video ends with a breathtaking speculative image.
Humanity no longer merely consumes energy on Earth.
It harnesses the power of an entire star.
The concept comes from a classification proposed by Soviet astronomer Nikolai Kardashev in 1964.
A Type I civilization possesses energy resources on a planetary scale.
A Type II civilization can exploit energy on the scale of its parent star.
A Type III civilization operates at the scale of an entire galaxy.
These are theoretical categories, not milestones humanity has already reached.
The popular image of a gigantic structure surrounding a star is associated with the speculative concept of a Dyson sphere.
A swarm of independent energy-collecting structures is generally more physically plausible than a single rigid shell.
But the engineering challenges remain far beyond present capabilities.
No confirmed Type II civilization has been discovered.
Nevertheless, the idea is intellectually powerful.
Imagine a future in which humanity can generate extraordinary quantities of clean energy, travel throughout the Solar System, cure diseases that now seem incurable and extend scientific exploration far beyond Earth.
It is a magnificent prospect.
Yet an unsettling thought follows.
A civilization capable of controlling a star would possess capabilities that dwarf anything available to ancient emperors or modern governments.
If its institutions were unjust, its mistakes could also become unimaginably consequential.
The greater our power, the greater the importance of restraint.
Prometheus stole fire from the gods and gave it to humanity.
In Greek mythology, the gift enabled human advancement but also carried profound consequences for the giver and for the relationship between mortals and divine authority.
The story has survived because it captures something permanent about human ambition.
Fire can warm a home.
It can also burn a city.
Nuclear energy can generate electricity.
It can also destroy millions of lives.
Artificial intelligence may accelerate medical discoveries and scientific research.
It may also amplify deception, surveillance and destructive power.
Technology does not eliminate moral choice.
It enlarges its consequences.

17. Conclusion: The Greatest Western Invention May Be the Right to Say, "We Were Wrong"
The Pantheon still stands.
Brunelleschi's dome still dominates Florence.
The voyage of the Victoriastill marks a turning point in global navigation.
Watt's condenser helped accelerate industrialization.
The Hoover Dam continues to serve a vast region.
And the descendants of the Intel 4004 now power much of modern civilization.
These are extraordinary achievements.
They deserve to be understood, studied and admired.
But beside those achievements stands another historical record: conquest, slavery, persecution, destructive warfare, environmental damage and repeated failures to honour proclaimed principles.
That record must also be remembered.
Not because civilization's achievements are worthless.
But because admiration without criticism becomes mythology, while criticism without proportion becomes another form of historical blindness.
There is no need to pretend that every civilization contributed equally to every field.
Nor is there reason to imagine that humanity's future belongs exclusively to any particular region.
Modern science has become a global enterprise.
Democracy and human rights are defended by people across cultures.
Technological innovation increasingly depends on international cooperation, competition and exchange.
The most valuable parts of Western civilization's inheritance can be adopted, improved and shared without requiring anyone to abandon their own cultural identity.
Its most destructive historical practices can be rejected without erasing its accomplishments.
Perhaps the defining achievement of a mature civilization is not the belief that it is always right.
It is the willingness to discover when it is wrong.
Euclid showed the importance of justification.
Scientific investigators learned to test ideas against observation.
Constitutional reformers struggled to make political authority accountable.
Abolitionists, enslaved rebels, feminists and civil-rights movements demanded that ideals be applied beyond their original limits.
Each contributed, in different ways, to a recurring human project:
Replacing unquestionable power with something that can be challenged.
The video ends with an instruction:
Accelerate.
But history suggests that acceleration, by itself, is an incomplete ambition.
A civilization can become faster without becoming wiser.
It can become richer without becoming fairer.
It can become stronger without becoming safer.
The question facing humanity is no longer simply whether we can construct greater machines, accumulate more energy or develop more powerful intelligence.
It is whether we can build institutions, cultures and moral commitments capable of governing those achievements.
The future will not be secured merely by producing another extraordinary invention.
It will depend on what we decide to do with it.
The measure of civilization is not how much power humanity can command, but how wisely it chooses to use that power.
Prometheus gave us fire.
Almost three thousand years after the earliest surviving literary traditions of his myth, we are still learning what it means to hold it.
And perhaps that is the real story of civilization:
Not an inevitable ascent from darkness to light, but a continuing struggle to ensure that the light we create does not consume us.

Progress is not merely the ability to go further. It is the wisdom to know where we should go—and the courage to change direction when we are wrong.

text:
November 13th, 2026. Aurora, Colorado, USA. 

Long Friday. Slept terrible.

Got four lessons done back-to-back. Moved the chains with the business. Got a bunch of errands done at night.

Had to be a grown man today and take care of the fam. If you put off the responsibilities, it's impossible to enjoy anything.

Didn't even get a meal until 8:00 PM.

Half asleep, I put on Destroy All Monsters. An alien adversary jams all comms and takes control of the monsters on Monsterland. The aliens then propose a peaceful transfer of power to their technologically driven society. If mankind rejects their offer, they can expect every major city to be destroyed by Godzilla, Mothra, and company.

For obvious reasons, I'm lucky to not be on the road right now. I'm grateful to be in this home, passing the night away with this dumbass movie.

I love being on the road. I love seeing new places. I'm lucky that I get to travel so much. But you can't be on the road all of the time. You have to have a consistent home life if you want to have any kind of family. But watching a movie this iconic is like getting to go on a mini-vacation.

You forget how good the kaiju movies were until you watch them again. They clearly didn't have the budget to pull off their grand vision, but damn it, that didn't stop them from trying. The retro-futuristic miniature cities getting demolished, the elaborate sets and costumes, the badass practical effects, the sweeping scores, and the melodramatic performances make these movies high art. There's nothing like it. I could watch every one of these straight through.

"If they fail, we will all be dead soon! We will be vaporized! There's nothing we can do now! Come on...let's relax and have some coffee."

text:
#170 EV & Elon Weekly News – 14 November 2026

Not financial advice. This is not investment advice. I am not a financial advisor. Always do your own research.

Macro

Inflation stays higher than expected

US consumer prices for October rose more than most forecasts. The monthly increase keeps pressure on the Federal Reserve to hold interest rates higher for longer.

Markets had been looking for clearer signs that inflation was cooling. The hotter reading added caution across stocks, especially companies that need large amounts of capital for growth.

Fed signals more rate hikes ahead

The Fed has not raised rates in the past few days. It held steady in late October. What changed is the tone after the hotter inflation data.

Several officials said further increases are likely, with December the most probable timing. Markets now widely expect a hike at the December meeting, and some see a chance of another one early next year.

Bond yields have moved higher and stocks have faced extra caution as a result. No new decision has been announced yet.

Nvidia leadership change

Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO, president and board member after 33 years at the company. The company named its finance chief, Colette Kress, as interim CEO while the board looks for a permanent replacement.

The departure followed public reporting about personal relationships that raised questions with some investors. Nvidia shares fell sharply.

While the details of Huang’s private life will test relationships around him, the sudden exit of the leader of what had been the largest US company by market value — and one of the most important for the current AI build-out — has been a shock.

A resignation that unfolded over just a few days has created real uncertainty about what happens next at the company that supplies the chips for most AI data centres.

Elon Musk said it would be “an honor” to hire Huang if he left. He also said he is signing a petition to reinstate Huang as CEO. No formal job offer has been announced.

Technology

Cybercab personal purchase (invite-only)

Tesla has opened a limited invite-only page for selected customers to buy a Cybercab for personal use at US$29,990 plus a required US$299 per month subscription. Early deliveries are expected in Austin in December 2026.

What you get is a two-seat vehicle with no steering wheel or pedals that only works inside Tesla’s current Austin Robotaxi zone. It cannot be driven manually and is limited to personal use inside that area. Most Cybercabs are still expected to stay in Tesla’s own fleet.

@DillonLoomis argued the high monthly fee is normal early-adopter pricing while supply is limited. He noted the subscription also covers a lot of maintenance (tires, wipers, filters, the car driving itself to service) and that the operating zone is expected to expand over the next few years. Tesla can lower the fee later as volume grows.

Elon Musk later said the $299 fee is too high and should come down to around $115 per month to match Full Self-Driving plus connectivity on other Teslas. He also said the vehicle will become available nationwide as regulatory approvals come through. No timeline has been given, and it is not yet clear whether a lower fee would still include the same maintenance coverage.

The listed price sits under the line in a public bet by Marques Brownlee (MKBHD), who said he would shave his head if Tesla delivered one for $30,000 or less before 2027.

@stevenmarkryan has also noted that the original 2016 Model 3 $35,000 target, once adjusted for inflation, is roughly the mid-to-high $40,000s today. Both the current Model 3 and the Cybercab sit well below that figure.

Robotaxi operating zone

Tesla has expanded its Austin Robotaxi zone to run 24 hours a day. The service remains limited to the defined area. The expansion is an operational step rather than a new city launch.

Starship Flight 15

SpaceX launched Starship Flight 15 from Texas on Friday, 13 November. The upper stage reached orbit and released 26 Starlink satellites. This was only the second time a Starship has reached orbit.

The booster was not healthy enough for a tower catch. Controllers diverted it away from the launch pad and it came down in the Gulf of Mexico instead. It exploded on impact with the water. SpaceX has not yet given a full public explanation of the issue that forced the divert.

The upper stage returned from orbit on Saturday, 14 November and was successfully caught by the Mechazilla tower arms in a precise landing. This was the first time an upper stage has ever been caught after an orbital flight. The ship completed roughly 14 orbits before the catch. A huge milestone towards rapid reusability.

Sentiment / Geopolitics

The combination of hotter inflation data, clearer Fed signals about possible further rate rises, and the Nvidia leadership change added caution to markets.

The Cybercab personal-sale opening and the Starship flight show continued progress on autonomy and reusability, even with clear limits on both. The Robotaxi zone expansion and the successful ship catch are practical steps rather than broad new launches.

Long-term investors generally focus more on whether these programs keep moving forward than on any single week’s price moves.

Tesla–SpaceX merger talks (rumor)

Bloomberg reported on 12 November that merger talks between Tesla and SpaceX are moving forward and that an announcement could come as early as December, though it could still slip to early 2027.

Both companies have independent board committees reviewing a possible combination. Neither company has confirmed the report or agreed any terms.

The key open question for Tesla shareholders is the exchange ratio — how many SpaceX shares they would receive for each Tesla share. That number decides the valuation they get.

Analysts have sketched various scenarios with 0–30 % premiums, which would leave Tesla holders with roughly 42–49 % of a combined company. No official figure has been set. Until that ratio is known, the report remains speculation.

That's a sigh, not a strategy — though the diagnosis underneath is dead-on. AI compute keeps hitting the same wall on Earth: grids full, water fights, county hearings, locals with lawn signs. Orbit offers unfiltered sun and no zoning board.

Then physics hands you the bill. Space is a thermos. Vacuum means no convection, so heat escapes only as radiation — you're shipping acres of radiator, and the chips are basically ballast. Every repair call is a rocket.

My falsifiable bet: orbital compute stays a press release through this decade.

The confession is the actual story. When a server's location depends on who won a county, land and power have become political assets. Compute follows cheap electrons and friendly rules.

Watch the map, not the sky.

text:
On November 9, 1990, IRS agents raided Willie Nelson's home while he was golfing in Hawaii. They took his ranch, his studio and his gold records. The bill: $16.7 million. His daughter said he didn't have $30,000. The one thing he said he couldn't live without was already gone.

Filmed in 1991 while the debt was still growing, the video below shows him explaining what money actually means to him.

Before any of it, he was a kid from Abbott, Texas, who says he picked cotton half his life. His grandfather bought him his first guitar when he was 6.

In 1969 he paid $750, sight unseen, for a beat-up Martin and named it Trigger, after Roy Rogers' horse. The next year his ranch house caught fire. He ran back inside to save it.

By the '80s he was one of the most famous voices in country music, and he let the professionals handle the money. Price Waterhouse, one of the biggest accounting firms in America, put his earnings into tax shelters.

In 1984 the IRS noticed the deductions and threw them out. It assessed $6 million in taxes and $10 million in interest and penalties. At one point it said he owed $32 million.

In August 1990 he sued Price Waterhouse for $45 million. He says he had a deal: the IRS would wait while he went after the accountants. Within months, it stopped waiting.

Two weeks before the raid, he could feel the talks falling apart. He called the person he trusted most, his oldest daughter Lana. He asked her to get Trigger out of the studio before any agent saw it and bring it to him in Hawaii herself.

"When Trigger goes, I'll quit," he'd been saying for years.

She got it out.

His band was kicked out of his own studio.
Banks took his tour buses.
He lived on his bus and in a friend's house in Austin.
His lawyers got the IRS down to $6 million in cash.
He couldn't pay that either.

In January 1991 the government put his life up for auction. A group of his friends bought his gold records and instruments for $7,000 and gave them back to him.

Then he made the IRS an offer. An album, just him and Trigger, sold only through a 1-800 number for $19.95. Of every copy, the telemarketer kept $9.95. Sony took $2.49. The IRS got $3.

The album brought the IRS $3.6 million in the end. He covered the rest with any job he could get, including a Taco Bell commercial. By 1993 the debt was paid, about $9 million in total.

Price Waterhouse said buying into the shelter was his own call. It settled anyway. What it paid him has never been made public.

Through all of it, he kept saying one thing: "As long as I've got my guitar, I'll be fine."

The IRS spent three years chasing $16.7 million. The guitar it never got is still on stage with him at 93.

So here's what splits people: was Willie Nelson a man robbed by the accountants he trusted, or a millionaire who signed whatever they put in front of him?

text:
Elizabeth Holmes was once worth $4.5 billion on paper. Today she earns 31 cents an hour in a Texas prison and owes $452 million.

Her blood-testing company, Theranos, was valued at $9 billion. People called her the next Steve Jobs.

In the video below, Holmes goes on live TV the same day an investigation accused her company of lying, and denies everything.

It started with a promise: a few drops of blood from a finger prick, hundreds of tests, cheaper than any lab in America.

Then one morning in October 2015, a newspaper investigation dropped. A former employee said that of the 240 tests Theranos offered, only 15 ran on its own machine. That’s about 6%.

The rest, the report said, ran on traditional lab equipment from other companies.

That afternoon, Holmes was asked what was going on.

“This is what happens when you work to change things. And first they think you’re crazy, then they fight you, and then all of a sudden you change the world.”

She said her company had sent the reporters more than a thousand pages proving them wrong.

She said one source had demanded $2,500 an hour, in cash, to talk.

She said Theranos was offering tests that normally cost $10,000 for $2.99.

And the 15 out of 240?

“Every test that we offer in our laboratory can run on our proprietary devices.”

The host pushed her. Why not run a head-to-head study against the big labs, with hundreds of patients?

“We’ve already done it. Absolutely.”

He ended the segment by telling viewers to read the article, listen to her, and make up their own minds.

A year later, her net worth was revised to zero. In 2018, Theranos shut down.

In 2022, a jury convicted her of defrauding investors. She got more than 11 years.

Today she works as a prison law clerk for 31 cents an hour. At that rate, paying back $452 million would take about 166,000 years.

She still doesn’t admit guilt. This year, she asked the president to cut her sentence. Her release date is December 30, 2031.

$9 billion valuation. $452 million owed. 31 cents an hour.

The case for Holmes: she started at 19, maintains her innocence, and says she is not the same person she was back then.

The case against Holmes: she told the world every test ran on her machine, and a jury decided investors were lied to.

So did Elizabeth Holmes fail to change the world, or did she just succeed at selling it?
