text:
Jake Dickert moved his family eight times in nine years to become a head coach, and on Thursday he signed a long term deal to stop.

Wake Forest is 8 and 1 and ranked 13th in the College Football Playoff rankings. He is 17 and 5 there in less than two seasons, and his first year went 9 and 4, the most wins any first year coach has ever had at the school. His offense is ninth in the country, and his quarterback, Gio Lopez, has thrown 18 touchdowns against one interception.

So Florida State wanted him. That is one of the better jobs in the sport, it came open at the right time, and the reporting this week had him as the name they were circling.

He signed the extension instead. The deal also moves more money into the staff and roster pools, which is what decides whether a school this size can hold on to what it builds.

John Currie is the athletic director at Wake Forest.

"He has done an extraordinary job of inspiring belief among our players, fans and the entire Demon Deacon community."

His own note on X afterward was mostly about other people.

"such a high level of appreciation for everyone involved at Wake Forest."

He grew up in Waukesha, Wisconsin, where his father was a teacher who became a school administrator, and that job kept moving the family from one small Wisconsin town to the next. He moved six times before he was done with high school.

He played quarterback at Kohler High School, then went to Wisconsin Stevens Point, which is Division III, where he played quarterback and then receiver and took a math degree. He met his wife Candice there.

Then he started climbing. Graduate assistant at Stevens Point. Then North Dakota State. Then South Dakota. Then Southeast Missouri State. Then Augustana. Then Minnesota State. Then South Dakota State. Then Wyoming. Then Washington State in 2020, as the defensive coordinator.

That is the eight moves in nine years.

Partway through the 2021 season Washington State lost its head coach and handed Dickert the team on an interim basis. A month later they took the word interim off it.

"I feel like I prepared my whole life for that moment."

He stayed out there through the 2024 season, and then Wake Forest came and got him. He is Wisconsin through and through by his own description, and when somebody asked him a while back whether he had ever wanted the big city version of this life, the answer was short.

"God no, I'm a small town guy."

He and Candice have three children.

Six moves as a kid, because of his father's work. Eight more in nine years, because of his own. On Thursday he signed the kind of deal that means he does not have to do it again.

One of the goals & concept behind 'The Universal Launchpad' is that every time there's a new chain, an instant flood of launchpads gets in and confuses everyone.

Pangea's solution of including every new chain solves this, while also granting the eventual possibility of enabling launches on other "stablished" chains.

See an example of it: Imagine you launched on Elysium.

Not to bare any criticism, but the chain's spark did not last very long. If you launched on any launchpad on there, and had a serious project, most likely you'd be struggling by now.

However, with Pangea v4, you would be able to launch on Elysium and THEN enable SOL or BSC, in order to keep your project up to date where demand is.

There's no secret to it. Being able to automatically open up your project to any other chain is the clear future that we've decided to build.

However, these are still not our final steps. The Universal Launchpad is only the first Act of a much greater setup, as Vlad Tenev put it:

"The best infrastructure is invisible. Most people don't know which network their texts run on. Chains should get there too. Users should see assets, not plumbing."

The space will get there. Pangea is building it.

text:
Today is day 1 of defense industry unemployment…

I'm starting this series not only to keep myself accountable, but also to keep a record of what it truly takes to find a job in today's market, and in defense specifically.

I think a lot of people shy away from the embarrassment of job rejections, but I'd like to share my journey transparently to show that even when the path seems difficult, you are not alone.

My last search took a total of 3 months and 438 applications to land my first role in defense tech. Hopefully, with some experience under my belt in Digital Communications at @turbineonetech, and the connections I've made in D.C. over the past 5 months, the process will be a little easier this time.

For those who don't know my story: I started as a fashion influencer in LA, and through 3 years of hard work, Marketing Director roles in aviation and AI tech, and a Master of Science program at @usc focused on defense and national security, I was able to make the full-time transition into the defense industry!

Feel free to check out my last post for more context, but I cannot thank the community on X enough for the outpouring of support, whether that's making connections or flagging opportunities. People in defense are some of the most passionate and supportive people I've ever met. It truly means the world, working in defense has been my goal for so long, and losing my dream job after only 5 months has been heartbreaking.

So, for day 1 of unemployment, here's everything I've accomplished so far:
- 2 in-person meetings (both a direct result of my post on X, so a big thank you to those individuals, you know who you are)
- 2 phone calls with previous connections who heard the news and are sharing my resume wherever possible
- 2 outreach calls from a defense neo-prime to talk through their company structure and referrals
- 3 first-round video interviews (also a direct result of my post on X)
- 3 cold applications on LinkedIn

Every day I'll be sharing my stats to track my progress, so here are my day 1 results:
Total meetings: 9
Total applications: 9
Total rejections: 0
Total offers: 0
Total days unemployed: 1

If you or anyone you know is hiring in defense communications, marketing, social media, or information operations, please don't hesitate to reach out. I cannot stress enough how passionate I am about this industry.

Restarting my job search in a city I just moved to, in an industry I'm still new to, is both scary and intimidating. But here's to the start of a new journey, a new role, and continuing to find my place in this industry!

text:
Western Sahara🇪🇭 is a state colonized by Morocco. And before that, it was colonized by Spain.

In 1974, Spain agreed to organize a referendum. Morocco opposed it, and it never happened. Instead, in 1975, Morocco sent about 350,000 civilians across the border in the to claim land that wasn't its own. Tens of thousands of sahrawis fled the fighting.

Morocco then built a wall of sand and rock, lined with landmines, that splits the territory in two. Sahrawis on one side. The phosphates and the fish on the other.

In 1991, a ceasefire promised a referendum again. Thirty-five years later, it still hasn't happened. Morocco stalled over who gets to vote, and today it rejects any vote that includes independence as an option. Its only offer: autonomy, under Moroccan rule.

In 2010, Moroccan forces dismantled the gdeim izik protest camp, where thousands of Sahrawis were demanding basic rights. Activists were later sentenced to long prison terms, some up to life, after a military trial. Foreign journalists and observers have repeatedly been expelled.

This is what colonization looks like, whether it's done by a European power or by a neighbor. A people that is never allowed to vote on its own future is not free. And when the world only cares about occupations that are convenient to talk about, it chooses who counts as a victim.

Historically, the Sahrawi tribes have been far closer to Mauritania than to the Moroccan state. And for centuries, the ˆsharifian empireˆ itself showed little interest in this land. In the 1767 treaty of Marrakesh with Spain, the sultan reportedly refused to take responsibility for what happened south of the Oued Noun, because his authority did not reach that far. The region was left to tribes who governed themselves and answered to no central power. Morocco only discovered a sudden urge to claim this territory once Spain was on its way out, and once its phosphates and atlantic fisheries were known to be worth a fortune.

text:
Care outside VA facilities goes through the Community Care program (created/expanded by the 2018 MISSION Act). For the VA to pay, the veteran generally must:
Be enrolled in (or eligible for) VA health care, and
Get prior approval from their VA care team (except for emergencies and certain urgent care), and
Meet at least one of these criteria:
VA doesn’t offer the service needed
They live in a state/territory without a full-service VA facility
VA can’t meet access standards (typically 20-day wait / 30-minute drive for primary/mental health; 28-day wait / 60-minute drive for specialty care like surgery)
The veteran and their VA provider agree community care is in their “best medical interest”
VA quality standards aren’t met for that service
Certain grandfathered distance rules from the older Choice program
The provider usually needs to be in the VA’s Community Care Network (or have a specific agreement). Unauthorized care leaves the veteran responsible for the bill.⁠Va

Practical reality for surgery
Surgery is specialty care, so the same rules apply. Veterans who meet the criteria can often get VA-funded surgery at local private hospitals, but it is not an unrestricted “go anywhere” benefit. Emergency surgery is treated more flexibly (notify VA within 72 hours).

Otherwise,  if the VA is your insurance to cover the cost, the answer is  No. Veterans cannot simply pick any hospital or surgeon. Care outside VA facilities goes through the Community Care program (created/expanded by the 2018 MISSION Act). For the VA to pay, the veteran generally must:
Be enrolled in (or eligible for) VA health care, and
Get prior approval from their VA care team (except for emergencies and certain urgent care), and
Meet at least one of these criteria:
VA doesn’t offer the service needed
They live in a state/territory without a full-service VA facility
VA can’t meet access standards (typically 20-day wait / 30-minute drive for primary/mental health; 28-day wait / 60-minute drive for specialty care like surgery)
The veteran and their VA provider agree community care is in their “best medical interest”
VA quality standards aren’t met for that service
Certain grandfathered distance rules from the older Choice program
The provider usually needs to be in the VA’s Community Care Network (or have a specific agreement). Unauthorized care leaves the veteran responsible for the bill.⁠Va

Practical reality for surgery
Surgery is specialty care, so the same rules apply. Veterans who meet the criteria can often get VA-funded surgery at local private hospitals, but it is not an unrestricted “go anywhere” benefit. Emergency surgery is treated more flexibly (notify VA within 72 hours).

But you’d still better be at mandatory PT in the morning.

And you’d better not let your waist grow above standards

If command says you work through lunch, then you work through lunch, maybe with a few bites from a sodium-packed plastic MRE

You can complain. You can give a bad survey. But in the end this sort of thing happens ALL THE TIME, across every job the Army has to offer. And if you try to quit, or disobey, you face legal action. Either a discharge, which affects future employment, or actual jail.

text:
How the boots pass from hand to hand

In the Greek Library attributed to Apollodorus, Perseus obtains winged sandals from the nymphs as part of the equipment for his expedition. In Snorri’s Prose Edda, Loki wears shoes that let him run through air and over water when the dwarf Brokkr comes to collect on a wager. A medieval Indian tale gives this same power a particularly ingenious plot. In Somadeva’s Ocean of Story, two heirs quarrel over a vessel, a staff, and flying shoes. Putraka proposes a race to settle the dispute. The heirs run off, and he puts on the shoes and flies away with all three objects. His trick turns on a practical insight. As long as the footwear can change owners, speed is something a quick-witted stranger can acquire in the time it takes to put on a pair of shoes. 

Apollodorus, Library 2.4.2–3. https://t.co/U1ewMp2s8G⁠
Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Skáldskaparmál. https://t.co/BUxxj1bxaL⁠
Somadeva, The Ocean of Story, ch. 3, trans. C. H. Tawney. https://t.co/rJpFujGjVS⁠

That trick reappears in the Italian verse tale Historia di Lion Bruno, whose earliest known printing dates to Venice, 1476. Lion Bruno acquires boots and an invisibility cloak from three men disputing stolen goods. In the text edited by Ezio Levi, the enchanted boots allow the wearer to cammina come il vento, “walk like the wind.” They get Lion Bruno up a mountain to a hermit, who tells him to follow the sirocco to the castle of his lost beloved. Here speed gets him as far as the person who can give him directions. The wind first measures his pace. Then a particular wind shows him where to go. 

Alice Martignoni, “La Historia di Lion Bruno e la filologia dei cantari,” Filologia e Critica 43 (2018), pp. 96–111. https://t.co/LnjdNK9BpZ⁠
Ezio Levi, ed., Fiore di leggende, Liombruno, second canto, stanza 6. https://t.co/55OwQ7P57U⁠

Perrault measures the stride

There is a direct European witness to the comparison between Homer and the seven-league boots. Perrault made it himself. In his Parallèle des anciens et des modernes of 1692, a speaker compares the enormous bounds of Homer’s horses with the feats of ogres wearing seven-league boots. Andrew Lang calls attention to this passage in his edition of Perrault. Five years after that dialogue, Perrault published Little Thumb. In Sleeping Beauty, from the same collection, he gives the rule outright. A dwarf can cover seven leagues in a single step. At a four-kilometre league, that amounts to twenty-eight kilometres, or about seventeen miles, every time a foot goes down. The familiar unit makes the feat imaginable. The stride makes it fantastic. 

Charles Perrault, Parallèle des anciens et des modernes, vol. 3 (1692), p. 117. https://t.co/5XzKxsa37C⁠
Andrew Lang, introduction to Perrault’s Popular Tales. https://t.co/6ZMIWfbgOm⁠
Perrault, The Sleeping Beauty in the Wood. https://t.co/pxvR4mbDbD⁠

Little Thumb does more with the boots than run. When he tells the ogre’s wife a false story about her husband being captured, he shows her the boots as proof that the ogre sent him. She recognizes the object and grants its wearer the authority of its owner. Perrault then gives a second account of what the boy did. In that ending, Little Thumb goes to court and offers to bring the king news of an army two hundred leagues away before the end of the day. That is the point at which the ogre’s boots take on the old office of Hermes’s sandals. The boy who escaped a pursuer becomes a professional messenger. The two endings give the same possession different consequences. In one, someone recognizes the boots and believes the story that comes with them. In the other, the wearer earns his standing by going the distance and bringing back news. 

Perrault, Le Petit Poucet, the two endings. https://t.co/JsJU6DZiG4⁠

text:
That distinction Sanna Marin makes—between an aggressor ceasing its aggression and a victim surrendering its existence—goes right to the heart of moral clarity and living in truth.

In the language of Václav Havel and Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, demanding a "compromise" that erases a nation's right to exist is asking the victim to sign onto a lie just to make the room quieter for everyone else. 

Treating an invading army and an invaded country as morally equivalent at the negotiating table flattens reality—it replaces truth with convenience.

The parallel to personal life is striking too: true peace—whether between nations or inside a human soul—never comes from pretending a violation didn't happen or abandoning one's own right to exist just to stop the conflict.

This is what Vaclav Havel, play-wright, dissident, prisoner, and then president of the Czech Republic learned from his experience under Communist rule.  And he offered this experience to us in his speech to the US Congress in 1990:  "The specific experience I'm talking about has given me one certainty:  Consciousness precedes Being, and not the other way around, as Marxists claim.  For this reason, the salvation of this human world lies nowhere else than in the human heart, in the human power to reflect, in human modesty, and in human responsibility.  Without a global revolution in the sphere of human consciousness, nothing will change for the better...and the catastrophe toward which this world is headed...will be unavoidable."

A decent amount of parts are interchangeable and I can only assume your reasoning for (rather arrogantly) asserting this is a 240L is that it has a SHOULDER THING THAT GOES UP, which, again, is an interchangable part between the 240s, and the USMC has been outfitting more and more 240Bs with the exact same collapsible stock as is on the 240L and not the traditional plastic oar.

The USMC has repeatedly turned down offers to buy the Lima and it is not believed that they are suddenly making a 180° change in their disinterest for it since 2010, when they decided ~5.5lbs wasn't worth the price (they're Marins, dagummit), again in 2011 they even doubled down by suggesting the possibility of adding MORE weight with suppressors and such to the 240B.

text:
This is a post for those worried about a grid collapse who live in an apartment in a big city.
 
Listen, living off-grid is great, and the people who do it are ahead of their time. But not everyone can prepare like that, and I worry about those who are in vulnerable situations.    

I am posting this so others who live in cities can learn how to prepare themselves and not panic that they don't have homesteads or the ability to live off-grid.  

Yes, in a perfect world living off-grid is a great way to address a grid shutdown, but if you can't uproot your life to get there—this is for you. 

I am NOT an expert prepper by any means. Just a woman trying to prepare as best I can for what might be coming. 

For those who live in cities, there is a lot you can do to prepare yourself.
 
The first thing is don't panic (doesn't help anything) and just get organized. 

I have done my best to prepare, as living off-grid in my late sixties is not an option (as much as I would like it to be).

Here is my list. It might not be the best list, but it's a good start. 

Here is my list: 

1. Power 

I have a generator (mine is the first on the list)

- Best Apartment Generator Overall: Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 (1,070Wh, 1,500W output, 23.8 lbs). It offers the best balance of proven reliability, capacity for 1-2 bedroom essentials, and portability.    

- Best Overall Balance: The EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus (1,024Wh, 1,024W output) is highly rated for its fast charging, sub-10ms UPS switching (which keeps refrigerators and routers alive during power dips), and ample outlets for apartment essentials.

- Best Value for 1-Bedrooms: The Bluetti AC70 (768Wh, 1,000W output) offers a LiFePO4 battery that lasts up to 10 years and can power a one-bedroom apartment's essentials for 18–24 hours at a lower price point.

I have backup battery power strips that work for a while after power goes out.     super sunny). These can power my phone and laptop as needed. 

I have backup battery power strips that work for awhile after power goes out.     

I survived Hurricane Sandy (2 weeks without electricity) and the NY blackout prior. I remember it well, and as long as it’s not frigid temperatures, you can get through it. Of course, if the grid goes down, life won't be easy, but you can do a lot now to get through it.

2. Food: 
I have 1-2 years of food (freeze-dried food and 20 lb bags of beans and rice with large tins of olive oil, nuts, seeds, seed butter, powdered milk, and eggs if I need them etc. 

3. Water 
I have 20-5 gallon jugs of distilled water, and over 10 cases of spring water. 

4. Grow Your Own Food
I have pots in my windows to grow food - lettuce, garlic, herbs etc. Start now. 

5. Communication 
I have an old-style wall phone plugged into the wall that survives grid collapse (until utility generators burn out).

For those that have the ability to be off-grid absolutely listen to your off-grid experts like @healthnutnews - she of all people is the expert to guide you there.

I just worry about those who are not able to set themselves up like that at this point in time. 
 
My ONLY purpose in posting this is for those who are not able to make a change in their lifestyle and may be panicking. 

Please share any other tools you can think of below!

text:
⚡ SNF PULSE™   

SPACE INFRASTRUCTURE & LAUNCH ECONOMICS

SPACEX CAUGHT STARSHIP AFTER 14 ORBITS. THE NEXT TEST IS REFLYING IT.

SpaceX has achieved one of the most important technical milestones in the development of its Starship launch system.

On Saturday, November 14, Starship returned from orbit and was captured by the mechanical arms of its launch tower in Texas.

The spacecraft spent approximately 22.5 hours in flight, completed 14 orbits around Earth and deployed 26 next generation Starlink satellites.

It then survived atmospheric reentry, executed its powered descent and returned to the launch site.

This is the first successful tower capture of a Starship upper stage returning from space.

The achievement matters because recovering a spacecraft is a prerequisite for reusing it.

But the mission also demonstrated why full rocket reusability remains difficult.

🟨 WHAT CHANGED

🟢 Starship Flight 15 successfully returned its upper stage from orbit.

🟢 Ship 42 was captured by the launch tower at Starbase, Texas, Saturday afternoon.

🟢 The spacecraft completed 14 Earth orbits during approximately 22.5 hours of flight.

🟢 SpaceX deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites during the mission.

🟢 The spacecraft's thermal protection system performed successfully through reentry.

🔴 The Super Heavy booster catch was aborted during Friday's launch.

🟡 Its recovery sequence ended in the Gulf of Mexico after the booster failed to meet the conditions required for a safe tower catch.

🔴 The underlying booster failure remains under investigation.

The result is a major recovery milestone, but not a complete demonstration of both rocket stages being recovered on the same flight.

🟨 WHY THE CATCH MATTERS

Traditional orbital launch systems generally discard significant hardware after each mission.

That creates an expensive recurring manufacturing requirement.

Reusable rockets seek to change that economic structure by recovering flight hardware, inspecting it, refurbishing it and eventually flying it again.

SpaceX has already demonstrated the commercial importance of booster reuse through Falcon 9.

Starship is designed to extend the principle to the entire launch system.

Recovering the upper stage is particularly difficult.

It must survive orbital flight, intense atmospheric reentry heating and a precisely controlled return to its launch site.

Saturday's capture demonstrates that these systems can operate together successfully during an orbital mission.

That removes an important technical uncertainty.

But a successful catch is not the same as a successful reflight.

🟨 THE ECONOMIC QUESTION

The investment case for a fully reusable orbital rocket depends on much more than landing.

Recovered hardware must remain suitable for subsequent missions.

Inspection and refurbishment must be manageable.

Launch turnaround times must improve.

And the cost of recovery and reuse must eventually justify the complexity of the system.

A spacecraft that returns successfully but requires extensive rebuilding may still offer limited economic advantages.

A spacecraft that can return, receive modest servicing and fly repeatedly could fundamentally change launch capacity and cost structures.

Saturday demonstrated recovery.

The next important evidence will come from what SpaceX can do with the recovered vehicle.

🟨 STARLINK AND COMMERCIAL CAPACITY

The mission also deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites.

That makes Flight 15 more than an engineering demonstration.

The launch supported SpaceX's expanding communications infrastructure while testing the transportation system intended to sustain it.

Larger satellite constellations require dependable launch capacity.

They also require the ability to replace aging satellites and expand network capabilities over time.

If Starship eventually supports more frequent and economical launches, it could improve SpaceX's ability to deploy and maintain future satellite infrastructure.

The implications extend beyond broadband.

Space based communications, remote sensing, scientific missions and proposed orbital computing systems could all benefit from greater launch availability.

But commercial demand, regulatory approvals, operating economics and actual flight cadence will determine how much of that potential becomes realized business activity.

🟨 THE NASA CONNECTION

Starship is also central to NASA's lunar exploration plans.

A modified version of the spacecraft is intended to support Artemis astronaut landings.

That creates an important distinction between commercial development and government mission requirements.

SpaceX's successful upper-stage recovery advances confidence in the spacecraft's engineering capabilities.

But a lunar mission requires additional demonstrations.

Orbital refueling, extended space operations, mission reliability and crew safety remain essential.

Saturday's result strengthens one part of the technical foundation.

It does not complete the full Artemis development program.

🟨 WHAT SNF IS WATCHING

The postflight inspection of Ship 42.

Whether the recovered upper stage can be refurbished and flown again.

The final investigation into Super Heavy's failed recovery.

The next attempt to recover both stages on one mission.

Starship turnaround times and launch frequency.

Additional Starlink V3 deployment milestones.

NASA's orbital demonstration and lunar lander requirements.

Launch infrastructure expansion in Texas and Florida.

Actual recovery and refurbishment costs.

And whether repeated successful missions begin to establish a commercially sustainable model for full rocket reuse.

🟨 SNF LENS™

🟢 SIGNAL: SpaceX successfully captured a Starship upper stage after an orbital mission, demonstrating a major element of its intended reusable launch architecture.

⚪ NOISE: Claims that one successful upper-stage capture proves fully reusable Starship operations or guarantees dramatic reductions in launch costs.

🟡 CONFIRMATION: Successful inspection, refurbishment and reflight of recovered hardware, followed by reliable recovery of both stages.

🔴 RISK: Booster recovery failures, thermal protection challenges, refurbishment complexity, operational delays and slower than expected improvements in launch economics.

🟨 THE BOTTOM LINE

SpaceX has crossed an important technical threshold.

Starship has now completed an extended orbital mission, deployed satellites, returned through Earth's atmosphere and been physically captured at its launch site.

That is a meaningful achievement.

But aerospace economics are established through repeatability, not isolated demonstrations.

Recovering a rocket is the first step.

Reusing it safely, frequently and economically is the next.

For investors watching commercial space infrastructure, Saturday's milestone narrows the gap between technical ambition and demonstrated capability.

The remaining question is whether SpaceX can turn successful recovery into a repeatable transportation system.

That is where the next stage of economic value will be tested.

Touring as a comedian isn't just about getting on stage and telling jokes. It's also about experiencing different cities, meeting different audiences, and learning how people respond to humor in different places.

Nikki Glaser's stories about road trips, college crowds in the Midwest, and Florida offer a glimpse into the unpredictable life of a touring comedian.

Every crowd has its own personality. What gets a huge laugh in one city might receive a completely different reaction somewhere else.

That's the challenge of live comedy: you have to read the room, trust your material, and adapt to the audience in front of you.

text:
Vile woman offers sex, fakes a broken shoulder and threatens the deputy taking her in.

Florida, 2026. An elderly man recovering from a stroke let a woman he knew stay at his place. Her parents had kicked her out and he felt sorry for her. It lasted one day. He says she got drunk, screamed in his face all day, threw things at him, took his pills and then drove off in his car even though she has no license. When deputies arrived, his face was beaten and his ear was bleeding.

She is sitting at the neighbor’s house telling a very different story. She says he demanded sex in exchange for a place to stay, and that she was tied up and held in a room. The story changes every five minutes. The deputy asks simple questions: what year is it and who is the president. She gets the year right but can’t come up with the president, and just says all politicians are ugly.

Asked if anything physical happened, she says nobody touched anybody. Then she is told she’s under arrest for battery, and the show begins. She screams that her arm is broken and she just had surgery. She yells that her father was a cop for 40 years and will have everyone fired. She kicks a deputy and picks up a second charge, battery on a law enforcement officer.

In the patrol car it gets worse. She promises to knock the deputy’s eyes out and tells her to keep them closed when she sleeps. She says women only take this job because no man wants them. Then she moves on to crude sexual offers. When none of that works, she suddenly screams that she is having a seizure and can’t breathe.

After that she drops to the floor of the car, demands a lieutenant and spits toward the deputies. Paramedics arrive and still offer to take her to the hospital to check that shoulder.

Do people like this need treatment or jail?

text:
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

Earlier this year, when I realized how ridiculously easy generative AI has made it to manipulate people’s images, I maxed out the privacy settings on my social media accounts and swapped my Facebook and Twitter profile pictures for illustrations of myself.
 
The revelation came after playing around with Stable Diffusion–based image editing software and various deepfake apps. With a headshot plucked from Twitter and a few clicks and text prompts, I was able to generate deepfake porn videos of myself and edit the clothes out of my photo. As a female journalist, I’ve experienced more than my fair share of online abuse. I was trying to see how much worse it could get with new AI tools at people’s disposal.

While nonconsensual deepfake porn has been used to torment women for years, the latest generation of AI makes it an even bigger problem. These systems are much easier to use than previous deepfake tech, and they can generate images that look completely convincing.

Image-to-image AI systems, which allow people to edit existing images using generative AI, “can be very high quality … because it’s basically based off of an existing single high-res image,” Ben Zhao, a computer science professor at the University of Chicago, tells me. “The result that comes out of it is the same quality, has the same resolution, has the same level of details, because oftentimes [the AI system] is just moving things around.” 

You can imagine my relief when I learned about a new tool that could help people protect their images from AI manipulation. PhotoGuard was created by researchers at MIT and works like a protective shield for photos. It alters them in ways that are imperceptible to us but stop AI systems from tinkering with them. If someone tries to edit an image that has been “immunized” by PhotoGuard using an app based on a generative AI model such as Stable Diffusion, the result will look unrealistic or warped. Read my story about it.

Another tool that works in a similar way is called Glaze. But rather than protecting people’s photos, it helps artists  prevent their copyrighted works and artistic styles from being scraped into training data sets for AI models. Some artists have been up in arms ever since image-generating AI models like Stable Diffusion and DALL-E 2 entered the scene, arguing that tech companies scrape their intellectual property and use it to train such models without compensation or credit.

Glaze, which was developed by Zhao and a team of researchers at the University of Chicago, helps them address that problem. Glaze “cloaks” images, applying subtle changes that are barely noticeable to humans but prevent AI models from learning the features that define a particular artist’s style. 

Zhao says Glaze corrupts AI models’ image generation processes, preventing them from spitting out an infinite number of images that look like work by particular artists. 

PhotoGuard has a demo online that works with Stable Diffusion, and artists will soon have access to Glaze. Zhao and his team are currently beta testing the system and will allow a limited number of artists to sign up to use it later this week. 

But these tools are neither perfect nor enough on their own. You could still take a screenshot of an image protected with PhotoGuard and use an AI system to edit it, for example. And while they prove that there are neat technical fixes to the problem of AI image editing, they’re worthless on their own unless tech companies start adopting tools like them more widely. Right now, our images online are fair game to anyone who wants to abuse or manipulate them using AI.

The most effective way to prevent our images from being manipulated by bad actors would be for social media platforms and AI companies to provide ways for people to immunize their images that work with every updated AI model. 

In a voluntary pledge to the White House, leading AI companies have pinky-promised to “develop” ways to detect AI-generated content. However, they did not promise to adopt them. If they are serious about protecting users from the harms of generative AI, that is perhaps the most crucial first step. 

Deeper Learning

Cryptography may offer a solution to the massive AI-labeling problem

Watermarking AI-generated content is generating a lot of buzz as a neat policy solution to mitigating the potential harm of generative AI. But there’s a problem: the best options currently available for identifying material that was created by artificial intelligence are inconsistent, impermanent, and sometimes inaccurate. (In fact, just this week OpenAI shuttered its own AI-detecting tool because of high error rates.)

Meet C2PA: Launched two years ago, it’s an open-source internet protocol that relies on cryptography to encode details about the origins of a piece of content, or what technologists refer to as “provenance” information. The developers of C2PA often compare the protocol to a nutrition label, but one that says where content came from and who—or what—created it. Read more from Tate Ryan-Mosley here.

Bits and Bytes

The AI-powered, totally autonomous future of war is here
A nice look at how a US Navy task force is using robotics and AI to prepare for the next age of conflict, and how defense startups are building tech for warfare. The military has embraced automation, even though many thorny ethical questions remain. (Wired)

Extreme heat and droughts are driving opposition to AI data centers 
The data centers that power AI models use up millions of gallons of water a year. Tech companies are facing increasing opposition to these facilities all over the world, and as natural resources are growing scarcer, governments are also starting to demand more information from them. (Bloomberg)

This Indian startup is sharing AI’s rewards with data annotators 
Cleaning up data sets that are used to train AI language models can be a harrowing job with little respect. Karya, a nonprofit, calls itself  “the world’s first ethical data company” and is funneling its profits to poor rural areas in India. It offers workers compensation many times above the Indian average. (Time) 

Google is using AI language models to train robots
The tech company is using a model trained on data from the web to help robots execute tasks and recognize objects they have not been trained on. Google hopes this method will make robots better at adjusting to the messy real world. (The New York Times)

text:
MIT Technology Review Explains: Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of technology to help you understand what’s coming next. You can read more from the series here.

When ChatGPT was first released, everyone in AI was talking about the new generation of AI assistants. But over the past year, that excitement has turned to a new target: AI agents. 

Agents featured prominently in Google’s annual I/O conference in May, when the company unveiled its new AI agent called Astra, which allows users to interact with it using audio and video. OpenAI’s new GPT-4o model has also been called an AI agent.  

And it’s not just hype, although there is definitely some of that too. Tech companies are plowing vast sums into creating AI agents, and their research efforts could usher in the kind of useful AI we have been dreaming about for decades. Many experts, including Sam Altman, say they are the next big thing.   

But what are they? And how can we use them? 

How are they defined? 

It is still early days for research into AI agents, and the field does not have a definitive definition for them. But simply, they are AI models and algorithms that can autonomously make decisions in a dynamic world, says Jim Fan, a senior research scientist at Nvidia who leads the company’s AI agents initiative. 

The grand vision for AI agents is a system that can execute a vast range of tasks, much like a human assistant. In the future, it could help you book your vacation, but it will also remember if you prefer swanky hotels, so it will only suggest hotels that have four stars or more and then go ahead and book the one you pick from the range of options it offers you. It will then also suggest flights that work best with your calendar, and plan the itinerary for your trip according to your preferences. It could make a list of things to pack based on that plan and the weather forecast. It might even send your itinerary to any friends it knows live in your destination and invite them along. In the workplace, it  could analyze your to-do list and execute tasks from it, such as sending calendar invites, memos, or emails. 

One vision for agents is that they are multimodal, meaning they can process language, audio, and video. For example, in Google’s Astra demo, users could point a smartphone camera at things and ask the agent questions. The agent could respond to text, audio, and video inputs. 

These agents could also make processes smoother for businesses and public organizations, says David Barber, the director of the University College London Centre for Artificial Intelligence. For example, an AI agent might be able to function as a more sophisticated customer service bot. The current generation of language-model-based assistants can only generate the next likely word in a sentence. But an AI agent would have the ability to act on natural-language commands autonomously and process customer service tasks without supervision. For example, the agent would be able to analyze customer complaint emails and then know to check the customer’s reference number, access databases such as customer relationship management and delivery systems to see whether the complaint is legitimate, and process it according to the company’s policies, Barber says. 

Broadly speaking, there are two different categories of agents, says Fan: software agents and embodied agents. 

Software agents run on computers or mobile phones and use apps, much as in the travel agent example above. “Those agents are very useful for office work or sending emails or having this chain of events going on,” he says. 

Embodied agents are agents that are situated in a 3D world such as a video game, or in a robot. These kinds of agents might make video games more engaging by letting people play with nonplayer characters controlled by AI. These sorts of agents could also help build more useful robots that could help us with everyday tasks at home, such as folding laundry and cooking meals. 

Fan was part of a team that built an embodied AI agent called MineDojo in the popular computer game Minecraft. Using a vast trove of data collected from the internet, Fan’s AI agent was able to learn new skills and tasks that allowed it to freely explore the virtual 3D world and complete complex tasks such as encircling llamas with fences or scooping lava into a bucket. Video games are good proxies for the real world, because they require agents to understand physics, reasoning, and common sense. 

In a new paper, which has not yet been peer-reviewed, researchers at Princeton say that AI agents tend to have three different characteristics. AI systems are considered “agentic” if they can pursue difficult goals without being instructed in complex environments. They also qualify if they can be instructed in natural language and act autonomously without supervision. And finally, the term “agent” can also apply to systems that are able to use tools, such as web search or programming, or are capable of planning. 

Are they a new thing?

The term “AI agents” has been around for years and has meant different things at different times, says Chirag Shah, a computer science professor at the University of Washington. 

There have been two waves of agents, says Fan. The current wave is thanks to the language model boom and the rise of systems such as ChatGPT. 

The previous wave was in 2016, when Google DeepMind introduced AlphaGo, its AI system that can play—and win—the game Go. AlphaGo was able to make decisions and plan strategies. This relied on reinforcement learning, a technique that rewards AI algorithms for desirable behaviors. 

“But these agents were not general,” says Oriol Vinyals, vice president of research at Google DeepMind. They were created for very specific tasks—in this case, playing Go. The new generation of foundation-model-based AI makes agents more universal, as they can learn from the world humans interact with. 

“You feel much more that the model is interacting with the world and then giving back to you better answers or better assistance or whatnot,” says Vinyals. 

What are the limitations? 

There are still many open questions that need to be answered. Kanjun Qiu, CEO and founder of the AI startup Imbue, which is working on agents that can reason and code, likens the state of agents to where self-driving cars were just over a decade ago. They can do stuff, but they’re unreliable and still not really autonomous. For example, a coding agent can generate code, but it sometimes gets it wrong, and it doesn’t know how to test the code it’s creating, says Qiu. So humans still need to be actively involved in the process. AI systems still can’t fully reason, which is a critical step in operating in a complex and  ambiguous human world. 

“We’re nowhere close to having an agent that can just automate all of these chores for us,” says Fan. Current systems “hallucinate and they also don’t always follow instructions closely,” Fan says. “And that becomes annoying.”  

Another limitation is that after a while, AI agents lose track of what they are working on. AI systems are limited by their context windows, meaning the amount of data they can take into account at any given time. 

“ChatGPT can do coding, but it’s not able to do long-form content well. But for human developers, we look at an entire GitHub repository that has tens if not hundreds of lines of code, and we have no trouble navigating it,” says Fan. 

To tackle this problem, Google has increased its models’ capacity to process data, which allows users to have longer interactions with them in which they remember more about past interactions. The company said it is working on making its context windows infinite in the future.

For embodied agents such as robots, there are even more limitations. There is not enough training data to teach them, and researchers are only just starting to harness the power of foundation models in robotics. 

So amid all the hype and excitement, it’s worth bearing in mind that research into AI agents is still in its very early stages, and it will likely take years until we can experience their full potential. 

That sounds cool. Can I try an AI agent now? 

Sort of. You’ve most likely tried their early prototypes, such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT and GPT-4. “If you’re interacting with software that feels smart, that is kind of an agent,” says Qiu. 

Right now the best agents we have are systems with very narrow and specific use cases, such as coding assistants, customer service bots, or workflow automation software like Zapier, she says. But these are a far cry from a universal AI agent that can do complex tasks. 

“Today we have these computers and they’re really powerful, but we have to micromanage them,” says Qiu. 

OpenAI’s ChatGPT plug-ins, which allow people to create AI-powered assistants for web browsers, were an attempt at agents, says Qiu. But these systems are still clumsy, unreliable, and not capable of reasoning, she says. 

Despite that, these systems will one day change the way we interact with technology, Qiu believes, and it is a trend people need to pay attention to. 

“It’s not like, ‘Oh my God, all of a sudden we have AGI’ … but more like ‘Oh my God, my computer can do way more than it did five years ago,’” she says.

text:
1. DEMAND FOR REINSTATEMENT
Elon Musk wrote on X yesterday he was signing an industry petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO—and the statement got 9.7 million views in a day.

The call started with staff at Huang’s company, Nvidia, but spread to the world, with Mainland Chinese and US patriots united in defence of the ousted leader.

If this happens, it would be a repeat of the Sam Altman story—which itself was a repeat of the Steve Jobs’ real life tale: a leader gets thrown out by a faceless board—but is eventually reinstated and ends up more powerful than ever.

But this may not be so straightforward: The board members are powerful, controlling a company with a valuation of $4 trillion (comparison: Canada’s GDP is $2.3 trillion). 

Also, the State Department (Marco Rubio), the Pentagon, and the CIA are all involved, and want to control the outcome for their own reasons. They want to see Nvidia as a weaponized part of the U.S. military machine.

.

2. 'SHE WAS NEVER A SPY'
Top U.S. officials and intelligence agencies are now rapidly backing away from the claim that Alice Huang Le was a Chinese spy. 

The U.S. Department of Justice is among them, with Attorney General Todd Blanche pointedly distancing himself from the assertion (Translation: “I didn't make it up, someone else did.")

President Donald Trump said in a podcast interview that it has "not yet" been determined if she was acting as a spy. Also, her “espionage” for the Chinese government is not on the agenda for his forthcoming meeting with President Xi Jinping (because there's no proof it ever existed).

Sources at the CIA, ODNI, and House Intelligence Committee have all expressed views admitting the lack of evidence for the spy label, according to CNN and multiple media outlets, and the Washington Post suggested Rubio exaggerated some CIA speculation.

.

3. OTHER US AI FIRMS WERE WORRIED
Industry insiders says Jensen Huang triggered concern from other big AI firms, who feared that he was moving to displace them, with Nvidia developing its own high-powered AI model – the Nemotron project.

Nvidia has already released several of its own AI models: The open-weight Nemotron 3 model family, including the 500B-parameter Nemotron 3 Ultra, which clearly posed a strategic and commercial threat to OpenAI and Anthropic.

Huang did not try to beat them at the API chatbot game, but took a more Chinese route. OpenAI and Anthropic were battling for the title of “world’s best performer” while the Chinese had aimed for a different target—“we’re the sweet spot where price and capability meet”.

Jensen Huang’s Nemotron 3 models like Nano (30B), Super (100B), and Ultra (500B), offered business customers high-performing, free or low-cost open-weight alternatives, in the Chinese style.

.

ECO-SYSTEM LOCK-IN FOR BUSINESSES
This meant big businesses worldwide would not have to pay the high costs of OpenAI and Anthropic. 

The cheaper alternative enabled them to own their models, and run them locally in their offices, or operate them via services like NVIDIA NIM. This had the further advantage of keeping sensitive data private in a closed loop.

Particularly worrying for Anthropic and OpenAI was the fact that Huang was visualizing an entire ecosystem that would lock in customers.

Nemotron could be purchased ready-packaged into an Nvidia software and hardware stack. It was known in the industry that even defense contractors such as Palantir, Booz Allen and Nvidia itself were looking to switch out of Anthropic and OpenAI models for this reason. 

They could escape data-retention security concerns by using an in-house Nemotron model instead.

This was an attraction in the eyes of Rubio and the armed forces, as one can imagine.
 
.

4. THE ISRAELI ANGLE
While social media is buzzing with talk about Israeli involvement in the affair, this needs to be put in proportion.

Yes, the interim CEO has strong connections with Israel—and there are other senior Israeli staff in the company.

But it has been true for years that Nvidia had a major Israel-based section, after it acquired that country’s chipmaker Mellanox in 2019. Nvidia has 6,000 people in Israel, representing around 13% of its global workforce. The country is known for its skilled tech-friendly workforce.

Still, the strong presence of people from the Israel lobby in the US tech business will remain an issue.

.

NEXT: Jensen Huang is due to be questioned by US politicians on December 3. He will not be looking forward to it.

Danger:  The U.S. House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party is getting into the game.

This is a notoriously McCarthyist group, known for its constant bleatings that everything from China is a national security threat to the United States. Chairman John Moolenaar has threatened subpoenas for testimony regarding Nvidia's safeguards against foreign adversary espionage.

This is bad news for all sides: The committee’s reductionist, over-hostile views inevitably end up harming the U.S. more than they harm China.

The story continues.
.

East Potomac Park covers approximately 327 to 330 acres on a man-made peninsula in Washington, D.C.
East Potomac Park and Hains Point
Total Park Size: Roughly 327 to 330 acres (though some historical or broader regional sources cite up to 400 acres).
Hains Point: A 15-acre open green space at the southern tip of the park, where the Potomac and Anacostia rivers meet.
Golf Course Area: The East Potomac Golf Links occupies about 210 acres of the park.
Recreational Space: Nearly 275 acres are dedicated to general recreation, including walking/bike paths, a swimming pool, and tennis courts.
Walking and biking loops around Hains Point
East Potomac Park and Hains Point offer golf, cycling, running, tennis, picnicking, swimming, fishing, and seasonal cherry blossom viewing, though the National Park Service does not publish exact weekend headcounts for the peninsula alone.

Things to Do and Enjoy
Golf and Driving Range: The East Potomac Golf Links features 36 holes across three public courses (the 18-hole Blue Course and two 9-hole courses), plus a 100-stall Toptracer driving range.
Historic Miniature Golf: Built in 1931, the Mini Golf Course at East Potomac Golf Links is the oldest continuously operating miniature golf course in the United States, featuring 18 D.C.-themed holes.
Biking, Running, and Skating: A flat, paved perimeter loop along Ohio Drive (roughly 3 to 4.4 miles depending on the route) hugs the waterfront and is heavily used by cyclists, runners, walkers, and inline skaters.
Waterfront Picnicking and Playgrounds: At the southern tip, the Point Picnic Area offers four reservable group picnic groves, grassy lawns, playgrounds, and panoramic views where the Potomac River, Anacostia River, and Washington Channel meet.
Tennis and Swimming: The northern end of the park houses the East Potomac Tennis Center, which offers 24 indoor and outdoor public courts, alongside an outdoor Olympic-size swimming pool open seasonally in the summer.
Fishing, Birding, and Sightseeing: Visitors frequently fish off the seawalls, watch planes land at nearby Reagan National Airport, ride the seasonal Wharf Jitney ferry across the Washington Channel, and walk beneath thousands of blooming cherry trees each spring.
Typical Weekend Crowd Levels: On standard weekends, the park draws steady crowds of thousands of local golfers, cyclists, runners, and picnicking families, peaking on Saturday afternoons. During major annual events—such as the National Cherry Blossom festival in spring, the Credit Union Cherry Blossom Ten Mile Run, and the Marine Corps Marathon weekend attendance surges into the tens of thousands.
Important Access Notice: Access to the park is currently subject to major disruption, as the National Park Service issued a directive to close all parkland and facilities south of Buckeye Drive—including Hains Point, the perimeter loop, and the golf courses—starting November 15, 2026, amid an active federal court battle over a proposed championship golf redevelopment.

text:
To receive The Algorithm in your inbox every Monday, sign up here.

Welcome to The Algorithm! 

Let me introduce you to Philip Nitschke, also known as “Dr. Death” or “the Elon Musk of assisted suicide.” 

Nitschke has a curious goal: He wants to “demedicalize” death and make assisted suicide as unassisted as possible through technology. As my colleague Will Heaven reports, Nitschke  has developed a coffin-size machine called the Sarco. People seeking to end their lives can enter the machine after undergoing an algorithm-based psychiatric self-assessment. If they pass, the Sarco will release nitrogen gas, which asphyxiates them in minutes. A person who has chosen to die must answer three questions: Who are you? Where are you? And do you know what will happen when you press that button?

In Switzerland, where assisted suicide is legal, candidates for euthanasia must demonstrate mental capacity, which is typically assessed by a psychiatrist. But Nitschke wants to take people out of the equation entirely.

Nitschke is an extreme example. But as Will writes, AI is already being used to triage and treat patients in a growing number of health-care fields. Algorithms are becoming an increasingly important part of care, and we must try to ensure that their role is limited to medical decisions, not moral ones.

Will explores the messy morality of efforts to develop AI that can help make life-and-death decisions here.

I’m probably not the only one who feels extremely uneasy about letting algorithms make decisions about whether people live or die. Nitschke’s work seems like a classic case of misplaced trust in algorithms’ capabilities. He’s trying to sidestep complicated human judgments by introducing a technology that could make supposedly “unbiased” and “objective” decisions.

That is a dangerous path, and we know where it leads. AI systems reflect the humans who build them, and they are riddled with biases. We’ve seen facial recognition systems that don’t recognize Black people and label them as criminals or gorillas. In the Netherlands, tax authorities used an algorithm to try to weed out benefits fraud, only to penalize innocent people—mostly lower-income people and members of ethnic minorities. This led to devastating consequences for thousands: bankruptcy, divorce, suicide, and children being taken into foster care. 

As AI is rolled out in health care to help make some of the highest-stake decisions there are, it’s more crucial than ever to critically examine how these systems are built. Even if we manage to create a perfect algorithm with zero bias, algorithms lack the nuance and complexity to make decisions about humans and society on their own. We should carefully question how much decision-making we really want to turn over to AI. There is nothing inevitable about letting it deeper and deeper into our lives and societies. That is a choice made by humans.

Deeper Learning

Meta wants to use AI to give people legs in the metaverse 

Last week, Meta unveiled its latest virtual-reality headset. It has an eye-watering $1,499.99 price tag. At the virtual event, Meta pitched its vision for a “next-generation social platform” accessible to everyone. As my colleague Tanya Basu points out: “Even if you are among the lucky few who can shell out a grand and a half for a virtual-reality headset, would you really want to?”

The legs were fake: One of the big selling points for the Metaverse was the ability for avatars to have legs. Legs! At the event, a leggy avatar of Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg announced that the company was going to use artificial intelligence to enable this feature, allowing avatars not only to walk and run but also to wear digital clothing. But there’s one problem. Meta hasn’t actually figured out how to do this yet, and the “segment featured animations created from motion capture,” as Kotaku reports. 

Meta’s AI lab is one of the biggest and richest in the industry, and it’s hired some of the field’s top engineers. I can’t imagine that this multibillion-dollar push to make VR Sims happen is very fulfilling work for Meta’s AI researchers. Do you work in AI/ML teams at Meta? I want to hear from you. (Drop me a line melissa.heikkila@technologyreview.com)

FAA Modernization: Follow the Money

✈️2019–2024: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy previously served on the advisory board of BGR Government Affairs, a Washington lobbying firm.

💰July 2025: Congress approved $12.5 billion to modernize the nation’s aging air traffic control system.

👀December 2025: The FAA selected Peraton, owned by private-equity firm Veritas Capital, over a competing IBM–Parsons team to manage the modernization project. Peraton’s contract had a $1.5 billion ceiling, with a negotiated price of approximately $876 million, to coordinate work by other contractors.

✈️March 31, 2026: Air Space Intelligence (ASI) contributed $2,500 to the congressional campaign of Sean Duffy’s son-in-law, Michael Alfonso. Lobbyists from Duffy’s former firm, BGR, separately contributed a reported $16,000 to Alfonso’s campaign.

💰June 22, 2026: The FAA awarded ASI a 12-year, $875 million contract for flight management technology, including its AI-supported SMART system. Federal records show 12 offers were received for the contract. ASI reported approximately $1.3 million in federal lobbying expenditures over 12 months and also hired Duffy’s former lobbying firm, BGR Government Affairs.

👀September 14, 2026: Federal auditors found that the FAA lacked a comprehensive cost estimate and coordinated schedule for its multibillion-dollar modernization project. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford had waived the lifecycle cost-estimate requirement, despite the risk of cost overruns and delays.

✈️September 21, 2026: ASI’s SMART system launched in the Washington, D.C., area. The AI-supported technology analyzes air traffic and recommends more efficient flight routes.

💰September 2026: The Modern Skies Act proposed another $30 billion for aviation modernization, including $600 million specifically for SMART and related flight management technology. This was proposed funding, not another $30 billion already spent.

👀October 9, 2026: Members of Congress called for a pause in SMART’s rollout, questioning safety testing, employee training, independent oversight, and a planned 90-day evaluation period. They also questioned whether normal safety and acquisition reviews had been shortened or waived. The air traffic controllers’ union reported it had not participated in SMART’s development, testing, or implementation.

✈️October 20, 2026: ASI announced a $325 million investment round at a $3 billion company valuation, approximately four months after receiving its $875 million FAA contract.

💰November 3, 2026: Sean Duffy’s son-in-law, Michael Alfonso, won the congressional election for Wisconsin’s 7th District, the seat Duffy previously held.

👀November 10, 2026: Just 50 days after SMART’s initial launch, the FAA announced nationwide expansion covering all 22 air traffic control centers, before the 90-day evaluation period referenced by Congress had elapsed. The FAA reported that SMART had helped reroute 180 flights, saving an average of 10 minutes and approximately 80 gallons of fuel per flight.

✈️November 13, 2026: Earlier that day, the administration requested $30.1 billion for aviation improvements. Later, a nationwide FAA communications failure grounded flights across the country. That evening, Duffy publicly declared: “The president has asked for $30 billion. I want $50 billion.”

⸻

👉Billions approved. Major private contracts. Political and lobbying connections. An accelerated AI rollout despite congressional concerns. Federal auditors warning about missing cost estimates and oversight.

👉Before Congress commits billions more, shouldn’t taxpayers know where the money is going, what has been accomplished, and who benefits?

text:
🇺🇦 Putin does not need a grand bargain in Shenzhen to claim a diplomatic victory. A photograph alongside Trump and Xi would already help him present Russia as an indispensable power, despite its continuing invasion of Ukraine.

The three leaders are scheduled to meet on 19 November alongside the APEC summit. Washington says nuclear arms and Iran are intended subjects, with Ukraine handled through a separate negotiating process. Reporting nevertheless indicates differences over the meeting’s scope.

Their interests diverge sharply.

Washington wants to manage several security challenges while concentrating resources on competition with China. Negotiation can reduce risks. But concessions that weaken allies would make American commitments less credible and future deterrence more difficult.

Moscow wants more than Ukrainian territory. Its demands seek to restrict Ukraine’s ability to defend itself and roll back NATO’s military presence in countries that joined after 1997. Putin is seeking political control over decisions that belong to Russia’s neighbours.

Beijing wants greater influence in Asia while preserving the trade and economic relationships on which its power depends. It has reasons to support Moscow, but those interests do not make China responsible for securing Putin’s preferred settlement.

Nor should Washington assume that accommodating Russia will detach it from China. Moscow’s dependence on Chinese markets, manufactured goods and technology gives that partnership substantial foundations. Putin can seek concessions from America while continuing to benefit from Beijing.

There are obstacles to a nuclear agreement too. China’s arsenal is considerably smaller than those of Russia and the United States. Beijing has resisted negotiations that it considers would entrench that imbalance. US officials themselves caution that no agreement is expected from this meeting.

A comprehensive division of the world into three stable spheres of influence therefore looks unlikely. But that should offer little reassurance to countries whose interests might be traded away through narrower deals.

A concession over Ukraine or NATO could damage European security without producing any lasting improvement in Russian behaviour. Beijing would also assess what such concessions revealed about Washington’s willingness to sustain its commitments. Taiwan’s circumstances are different, but the credibility of deterrence matters in both regions.

The comparison with Yalta has limits. Today’s leaders share neither a military victory nor an agreed foundation for a new international order. Their ambitions overlap and compete.

Yet an unsuccessful attempt at great-power bargaining can still harm the countries excluded from it.

The likelier outcome is continued competition punctuated by limited agreements. Arms-control measures, crisis communications and reciprocal restraint can be useful, provided they are verifiable and do not sacrifice other countries’ sovereignty.

Ukraine, Poland, the Baltic states and Taiwan are not bargaining counters. Their people have agency, interests and rights.

Diplomacy should reduce the capacity for aggression. It must not reward the aggressor with authority over its neighbours.

text:
Oh, all these fancy labels, "spinning" and "clarifying," I hope I can keep up!
You also have to realize something about how I work: I’m much more of a historian than a journalist, if you will. I present as much primary information as is needed to tell the full truth. 

I’m not a journalist trying to squeeze a catchy headline into a neat little box; that’s not me at all. So you’re actually right about one thing when a headline writer might use three words, I’m probably going to use ten, because I’m going to give you all the evidence sitting in the archive!

Look at what you’re really doing here: instead of simply welcoming more primary information so free people can read the records and decide for themselves, you automatically label the presentation of declassified documents as "spin." Not only is that pure subterfuge, you are doing your own spinning right here! Honestly, who is spinning? I’m getting dizzy just imagining you spin!

Let’s stick strictly to military records so you can see what declassification actually does. Take Navy Captain E. Royce Williams, who fought seven Soviet MiGs solo for 35 minutes near the Yalu River in 1952 and landed with 263 bullet holes in his jet. Because Washington classified the mission for 50 years, official records hid the truth until declassified files finally proved it and earned him the Medal of Honor. 

The same thing happened with Marine Force Recon Major James Capers Jr. in Vietnam and Master Sergeant Roy Benavidez in Cambodia: their heroics were buried behind classification stamps until declassified records finally set the record straight. 

Stop and ask yourself what if some of those classification stamps were slapped on those  files. Or any myriad of other files in the first place precisely because certain people in power did not want certain demographics to receive medals. Of course I’m just speculating, but that’s why I need more information. Information is always good. 

Who would reject more information . Ah yes see when you really want to spin . You want to limit information especially to the body politic.

Now, I am certainly not comparing the Till situation to their battlefield heroics; I am showing you what declassification actually does when official records have been hidden or distorted. As for what you call "settled," in history that often comes down to a person’s own bias, and there was plenty of racial bias baked into 1945 and 1955 military and courtroom files. I know firsthand from my family’s extensive history across World War II, Korea, and Vietnam that there are countless stories where the full truth may never be told. 

One of them was finally adjudicated regarding my mother’s brother before she passed away, she finally found out the truth of what really happened over there. He didn’t die in Vietnam, and his name isn’t on the Wall; he died after Vietnam, though he ought to be on the Wall because that war took him too. So I know firsthand how much it means to a family that gives its service when more truth finally comes out, and I’m sure you have service members in your own family that you’re proud of as well.

I’m a conservative; I don’t know where you stand, but I believe in freedom, and having more primary information out in the open is freedom! So feel free to dig into more information, and if you don’t actually want more information, then why even bother responding to me, except maybe to offer a critique? Which is fine, I really don’t mind a fair critique, though without engaging the records it makes the whole exercise kind of pointless. It sounds like you don’t really want information, friend; you just want intrigue!

Oh man, I went over the character limit again, gosh dang it!

Facta non verba veritas per tabulas apertas semper vincit. Take care!

text:
#NationsLeague
 (Matchday 5)

League A – Group 4

Portugal 1-4 Denmark

Denmark produced the result of the day. Højbjerg’s first-half penalty set the tone, then Rasmus Højlund took over after the break with two quick goals (49’ and 57’). Joachim Andersen added a fourth before Bernardo Silva scored a late consolation.
Portugal looked disjointed in their first competitive game without Cristiano Ronaldo. Denmark were clinical on the counter and superior in midfield control. This result keeps Denmark firmly in the fight to finish top of the group and reach the quarter-finals.hmm Ronaldo effect!

Norway 3-1 Wales

Antonio Nusa opened the scoring with a well-struck effort from the edge of the box (59’), Andreas Schjelderup made it 2-0 shortly afterwards, and Erling Haaland converted a late penalty (88’) for his 23rd Nations League goal. David Brooks pulled one back for Wales (79’).
Norway were dominant after the break. Wales created very little and remain in a difficult position in the group. Haaland continues to set records.

League B

Sweden 3-2 Bosnia-Herzegovina

Sweden raced into a 3-0 half-time lead (including two goals from Viktor Gyökeres, who extended his scoring streak). Bosnia fought back with goals from Armin Gigović and Sead Kolašinac, but Sweden held on.
This result confirmed Sweden’s promotion to League A. Gyökeres remains in outstanding form.

Austria 1-0 Republic of Ireland

Sasa Kalajdzic scored the only goal in the 78th minute. Austria were the better side throughout and deservedly secured promotion to League A with this narrow but controlled victory. Ireland struggled to create clear chances.

Northern Ireland 1-0 Ukraine

Terry Devlin scored the winner in the 68th minute. Northern Ireland produced a disciplined defensive performance and took their chance when it came. Ukraine dominated possession but lacked a clinical edge in front of goal. Important three points for Northern Ireland.

Romania 2-1 Poland

Alexandru Cicâldău (68’) and Dennis Man (72’) scored in quick succession for Romania. Marcel Reguła pulled one back late for Poland (82’).
Romania were clinical after the break and earned a valuable home win that keeps their hopes of a strong group finish alive. Poland were wasteful.

Georgia 0-2 Hungary

An own goal by Lasha Dvali (73’) and a late strike from Barnabás Varga (85’) gave Hungary a comfortable away win. Georgia offered little threat, and Hungary controlled the second half effectively.

Kosovo 0-0 Israel

A low-quality, tight contest with very few clear chances. Both sides cancelled each other out. Neither team will be satisfied with the point, but it keeps both in the middle of the pack.

text:
🚨JUSTICE FOR HEEHAW: A FORMAL REQUEST FOR AN INDEPENDENT INVESTIGATION 🚨

HeeHaw’s life mattered. So do the unanswered questions surrounding his death—and the way public agencies handled what followed.

In a formal complaint dated November 11, 2026,
journalist: Yanesky Frank-Holland asks the Georgia Bureau of Investigation to investigate the killing of the fifteen-month-old miniature donkey and the handling of the incident by multiple police departments, the Haralson County Sheriff’s Office, Rockmart Fire Rescue, the district attorney’s office, and the Georgia Department of Agriculture.

This request represents an enormous amount of research. According to the letter, Yanesky has assembled an archive of 672 files, including 437 radio recordings, and a seven-part case file with an exhibit index connecting the concerns to agency-produced records.
The complaint raises troubling questions:
It states that a body camera was activated twelve seconds after the fatal shot, with the preceding eighteen seconds preserved only as silent footage.

It identifies a use-of-force report confirmed to exist but not produced, along with an unproduced Taser deployment record. It also raises concerns about two drones that recorded nothing and flight maps produced from logs the fire department describes as unobtainable.

There is a deeply human concern here, too.
The complaint states that HeeHaw’s owner was never contacted at the scene or told where her animal’s body had been left. Imagine losing an animal you love and then having to fight for basic answers about what happened and where that animal was taken.
The letter also questions the documentation surrounding the district attorney’s review and the handling of public-records requests, including the continued withholding of HeeHaw’s necropsy. It notes that the same declination document cleared the officer and declined the case against the owner, setting aside another agency’s probable-cause finding against her.

Yanesky makes an essential point:
the GBI is being asked to examine the evidence without adopting any conclusion in advance.
The letter offers the complete archive and full cooperation, and lists copies for the Georgia governor’s office and attorney general’s office. This is a request for an investigation; the letter does not confirm that the GBI has opened one.
For everyone who has cared about HeeHaw, this complaint gives those unanswered questions a formal voice. A life was lost. The public deserves a careful, independent examination of the record—and answers supported by evidence.

❓ How do you feel knowing this complaint identifies reports that allegedly exist but still have not been produced?
❓ If HeeHaw had been your animal, how would you feel about the way the complaint says his owner was treated?
❓ Do you believe an independent GBI investigation would help restore public confidence in how this case has been handled?
❓ What would meaningful accountability and justice for HeeHaw look like to you?

text:
Madison Grant thought that the Nordic race was adapted for the specific climate of northern Europe and that when it strays outside of this zone it tends to degenerate, lose their virtues, and ultimately tend towards extinction. The "poor whites" of the south and the whites of the Caribbean are examples. A few select passages to illustrate:

"The race... always has been and probably always will be, adjusted to certain environmental conditions, chief of which is protection from a tropical sun. The actinic rays of the sun at the same latitude are uniform in strength the world over and continuous sunlight affects adversely the delicate nervous organization of the Nordics. The fogs and long winter nights of the North serve as a protection from too much sun and from its too direct rays."

"Scarcely less important is the presence of a larger amount of moisture but above all a constant variety of temperature is needed. Sharp contrast between night and day temperature and between summer and winter are necessary to maintain the vigor of the Nordic race at a high pitch. Uniform weather, if long continued, lessens its energy. Too great extremes as in midwinter or midsummer in parts of New England are injurious. Limited but constant alterations of heat and cold, of moisture and dryness, of sun and clouds, of calm and cyclonic storms offer the ideal surroundings."

"Where the environment is too soft and luxurious and no strife is required for survival, not only are weak strains and individuals allowed to survive and encouraged to breed but the strong types also grow fat mentally and physically..."

"Men of the Nordic race may not enjoy the fogs and snows of the North, the endless changes of weather and the violent fluctuations of the thermometer and they may seek the sunny southern isles, but under the former conditions they flourish, do their work and raise their families. In the south they grow listless and cease to breed."

"In the lower classes in the Southern States of America the increasing proportion of 'poor whites' and 'crackers' are symptoms of lack of climatic adjustment. The whites in Georgia, in the Bahamas and, above all, in Barbadoes are excellent examples of the deleterious effects of residence outside the natural habitat of the Nordic race."--Madison Grant, /The Passing of the Great Race/ (1916).
