text:
Here’s an explanation of the recent settlements in the recent media mass tort cases: the harm these o,ai tiffs experienced was c,aimed to be “negative body image, body dysmorphia, and depression/anxiety.” 

One might rightfully ask their parents why they allowed their children to access these apps at the age of 6, but that would place responsibility where it belongs instead of giving these MDL attorneys a narrative they created and plaintiffs they selected as “sympathetic plaintiffs ,” allowing the attorneys and states to extort these companies for millions and billions of dollars. A summary of one recent mass tort case ins the social media MDL:

The largest known amounts going to individual plaintiffs (not states or school districts) in the social media adolescent addiction mass torts are in the low millions per person, concentrated in carefully prepared bellwether/test cases.
As of mid-November 2026 (per Bloomberg Businessweek reporting on confidential deals, plus court outcomes):
•Roughly a dozen confidential pre-trial settlements with teen plaintiffs, most in the $2–2.5 million range per person.
•Meta agreed to pay two teens (S.J. and K.D.B.) a combined $7 million.
•TikTok paid four teens $2.5 million each; YouTube paid amounts in the ~$2–2.25 million range for several.
•The only individual case that reached a jury verdict (K.G.M. in Los Angeles Superior Court, March 2026) produced a $6 million award ($3M compensatory + $3M punitive) against Meta ($4.2M) and YouTube ($1.8M). Meta has appealed.

These figures come from the coordinated California state-court proceedings (JCCP 5255) and related federal MDL 3047 cases. Settlements typically include no admission of wrongdoing. By contrast, Meta’s August 2026 multistate AG settlement is up to ~$17.1 billion (mostly guaranteed installments over 10 years plus product changes), New Mexico’s penalty was $375 million (plus later abatement amounts), and one school-district bellwether (Breathitt County, KY) settled for a combined ~$27 million. Those go to governments or districts, not individual families.
Why the individual plaintiff amounts reach these levels (especially the highest ones)
These are bellwether/test cases selected and fully prepared for trial. In mass torts, such cases routinely settle for more than ordinary ones because:
•Defendants face elevated risk after the K.G.M. verdict (liability + punitives). Public trials expose internal documents (e.g., comparisons of app features to slot machines), put executives on the stand, generate intense media coverage, and create adverse precedents. Companies have shown strong preference for settling remaining early cases to avoid that.
•Plaintiffs and families also often prefer settlement. Trial is highly invasive for teens (defense scrutiny of private messages, mental-health history, usage details, etc.). Lawyers have described the offers as high enough that clients could not reasonably refuse, and some plaintiffs have dismissed claims specifically to protect privacy.
•Damages are tied to specific personal injuries (depression, anxiety, eating disorders, self-harm, etc.) for particular individuals, plus possible punitives. That is inherently more limited than the aggregated statutory civil penalties and public-nuisance/abatement claims available to states, or the systemic cost claims (counseling, disruption, etc.) available to school districts.
Cornell Law professor Alexandra Lahav has noted that prepared-for-trial cases tend to command higher settlements, while the thousands of other pending personal-injury claims are unlikely to receive comparable amounts (if they recover anything). There is still no global settlement or claims process for the individual personal-injury docket (thousands of cases remain pending in the federal MDL and California coordination).
In short, the largest individual amounts reflect the special economics and risks of early, fully worked-up test cases after an initial plaintiff verdict.

text:
Yes, the core story is true. It is based on Sen. Markwayne Mullin’s public testimony during his March 2026 confirmation hearing for Secretary of Homeland Security, as reported by multiple outlets including the Associated Press and Fox News.
Here’s the verified account:
•In January 2020, Mullin’s then-15-year-old son Jim (a competitive wrestler) suffered a severe traumatic brain injury in a wrestling incident. He nearly died, had an extremely low pulse, woke up after about 26 hours “a different kid,” with short-term memory loss, motor problems (couldn’t touch his nose, shuffled when walking), and difficulty with basic tasks like simple math. One of the few things he still knew was that Donald Trump was president.
•Trump called Mullin right away after hearing about it. He offered his private plane so the family could get to the Centre for Neuro Skills in Bakersfield, California, for specialized rehabilitation. Trump then called almost every day for roughly two weeks to check on Jim. Later, while on the 2020 campaign trail, Trump visited Jim in Bakersfield. When his staff repeatedly urged him to leave, he delayed departure (telling them the plane wouldn’t leave without him for at least another 15 minutes) and spent time with the boy. Mullin has said that interaction helped jog Jim’s memory and aided recovery.
•At the March 18, 2026, Senate hearing, Mullin became emotional (fighting back tears) while recounting this. He emphasized that Trump “didn’t do it for publicity” and acted because he cared, even during a tough election year. Jim later completed rehab and returned home; Mullin has spoken publicly about the experience before.
The viral post (in Spanish, credited to an Instagram account) closely tracks Mullin’s testimony and the contemporaneous news coverage. Some wording is dramatized for emotional effect (common in viral retellings), and the precise “why I love your dad… because he loves you” line is reported in connection with Trump’s interactions with Jim (sometimes tied to the visit or a later meeting), but the underlying events match what Mullin said under oath and what major outlets reported. Mullin was later confirmed as DHS Secretary.
In short, this is a real, documented account from Mullin’s own words, not a fabrication.

*BAKASSI PORT: NIGERIA’S GATEWAY* 

The Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of the Nigerian Ports Authority (NPA), Dr Abubakar Dantsoho, has said the Bakassi Deep Sea Port will significantly strengthen Nigeria’s position as a leading maritime gateway in West Africa and across the African continent.

He said the project, when completed, would transform Nigeria’s maritime landscape, boost regional trade, enhance connectivity with landlocked countries and attract greater investments into the nation’s blue economy.

Dantsoho stated this in a goodwill message at the Presidential Groundbreaking Ceremony of the Bakassi Deep Sea Port held on Friday.

According to him, the port is strategically designed to serve as a transformative maritime hub for Nigeria, the wider Gulf of Guinea and several countries in the Sahel region.

He explained that the project, being developed under a Public-Private Partnership (PPP) arrangement and backed by a $3.5 billion facility from the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank), would have the capacity to accommodate Ultra Large Container Vessels (ULCVs), reducing the need for frequent maintenance dredging.

The NPA chief executive said the port’s strategic location and supporting infrastructure would provide a competitive advantage for Nigeria in the international shipping and logistics industry.

He noted that, like the ongoing Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway, which is expected to improve connectivity and enhance port operations along the coastal corridor, the Bakassi Deep Sea Port would be supported by a dedicated 275-kilometre, six-lane Calabar-Ogoja-Gakem Superhighway.

According to him, the superhighway would bypass urban bottlenecks and establish a high-capacity evacuation corridor linking the port to Nigeria’s North-Central and North-Eastern regions.

He added that the road infrastructure would also position the port as a cost-effective transshipment gateway for landlocked countries, including Chad, Niger Republic, Mali and Burkina Faso.

Dantsoho stressed that the strategic significance of the project was further reinforced by the enormous trade and economic potential of landlocked countries in the region.

He said, “Africa accounts for 16 of the world’s 44 landlocked countries, with four located in West Africa. These include Mali, Niger, Burkina Faso and Chad, with a combined population of approximately 101 million people.

“The Bakassi Deep Sea Port therefore presents an important opportunity to strengthen regional trade connectivity, facilitate access to international shipping routes and position Nigeria as a preferred maritime gateway for the wider West and Central African markets.”

The NPA Managing Director emphasised the strong relationship between the size of a country’s economy, its population and the capacity of its seaports, noting that countries with large economies and populations often have major ports that serve as critical drivers of international trade.

Drawing comparisons with other economies, he cited the United States, which combines a large population and strong economy with major maritime facilities such as the Port of Los Angeles in California.

He also referenced Brazil, South America’s most populous country and largest economy, which is home to the Port of Santos, one of the continent’s leading maritime facilities.

He said the NPA was working towards positioning Nigerian ports as the leading maritime facilities in Africa, adding that achieving this ambition required sustained investment in infrastructure, modern technology and operational efficiency.

“The Brazilian experience offers an interesting comparison with Nigeria because both countries have ports with long histories. The Port of Santos is about 200 years old, while Apapa Port is approximately 100 years old.

text:
Thank you WeHo Online for republishing my op-Ed / open letter to the newly elected members of the West Hollywood City Council. As I said in my piece: 

You do not have to choose between being progressive and focusing on effective governance. There are certain realities we have to face that have nothing to do with ideology.

Homelessness is a crisis. Letting people live on the street the way they are, in unhealthy and dangerous encampments, is not humane. Nor is simply criminalizing them. We must strive, in a brave way that puts aside political ideology and political convenience, to actually find proven solutions based on data from other cities and places that are doing it right here in California such as San Jose and Redondo Beach — shelter, treatment, housing pathways, and accountability that works for the people living it and the neighbors living next to it.

It should not be considered (and IS NOT) conservative to support our small businesses as much as we can and to create a safe, clean streetscape where people feel they can walk down the block and business owners are not worried that someone is going to break in. These are not left-versus-right questions. They are questions of whether the City functions for the people who live and work here.

I am not a moderate on most issues. I am someone who believes more in getting progressive things done than in saying all the right things. While I did not endorse the winners in this race, I have served in appointed city government, local nonprofit leadership and have been involved in the civic and political life of this city for over a decade and a half. I offer my insight, support and help, because I love this city. I am hoping ideology and ambition can be set aside to address the severe challenges we face.

These are not challenges that should make us retreat to our political silos. We are all neighbors, literally. We all chose to live in West Hollywood because it is special and has unique strengths that we must fight to protect and preserve. This is not just a city. It is a symbol and a refuge, and it is so much bigger than it might appear.

A young man walked into his grandfather's house in California and found lawyers waiting for him. They said he'd leaked trade secrets and wanted him to sign papers. If he didn't, they'd sue.

His name was Tyler Shultz. His grandfather was George Shultz, a former US Secretary of State, and he sat on the company's board. The company was Theranos, valued at about nine billion dollars, with tests offered to real patients in Walgreens.

In the lab, Tyler saw tests failing quality checks and data being manipulated. He emailed Elizabeth Holmes. The company's president replied that if anyone else had sent it, he'd already have held them accountable for its "arrogant and patronising tone". Tyler quit that day, and his grandfather sided with Holmes. They didn't speak for months.

Tyler went to Wall Street Journal reporter John Carreyrou in secret. He refused to sign and wouldn't name anyone else. His parents talked about selling their house to cover the legal bills.

By 2018 Theranos was finished. In 2022 Holmes was convicted of defrauding investors and sentenced to more than eleven years.

George Shultz died the year before, at 100. He never apologised, but before he died they'd started to heal, and he said Tyler had shown great moral character, and that he'd made him proud 📚

Dear Wall Street 👋 @WSJ @markets @CNBC

One company is doing more than the other 24 combined 🚀

SpaceX flew 127 rockets this year. The other 24 rocket companies in the world flew 141 combined. But SpaceX carried about 78% of everything sent to orbit by weight. That's more than three times what all of them carried put together.

I live on the Space Coast. I hear the launches. I see them. I feel the rumble. This isn't numbers on a page from someone who wants Elon to fail. I watch it happen week after week. Unscripted. Real life.

You see a rocket company priced at about 60 times its sales. Main Street sees something bigger.

It has 11,000 Starlink satellites in space. Amazon has about 400.
Its new satellites carry 10 times more internet.
It owns an AI company.
It flies military missions and NASA astronauts.

That's not just a rocket stock. It's roads to space, internet from the sky and AI computers, all under one roof.

Judging it only on last quarter's sales is like judging the first railroad by its ticket stubs 🚂

Start from first principles. Count the factories, launch pads and satellites in the sky. Then do the math again.

A friendly word to money managers: in my view, pushing clients to dump SpaceX for a quick cash grab does our country no favors. Uncle Sam counts on SpaceX for national security launches, Golden Dome satellites and the only American ride for astronauts to the space station 🇺🇸

And to everyday shareholders: be bold. Call your advisor and ask what's being done with your SpaceX shares. Some accounts let a manager buy and sell without asking you each time. Know what's in your account. Ask questions. Speak up for what you want.

Not financial advice. Just a friendly nudge from the Space Coast  🚀

text:
SHE WANTED THE COPS TO MOVE THE PARADE CONES FOR HER CAR!!

Who is right, the officer who says the road is closed or the driver who says she has to get to work?

Police bodycam from a street festival in Laurel, Maryland. A woman asks officers to let her move the cones so she can drive out, they tell her the road is closed and offer to call her a taxi, and later she drives down the closed street and ends up under arrest.

I understand the frustration. Nobody wants to lose a shift because their street turned into a festival. But the moment she rolled into a road full of people on foot, this stopped being about her job. Those cones are there because people are walking where cars normally go. The officer apologized, explained, and offered her a ride. That is about as much grace as you can ask from somebody working a crowd. Picture walking that street with your little ones and seeing a car coming at you from behind the barricade. As parents, that is the part that settles it for us. Where she does have a point: residents should get real notice and a way out when a city closes their street, and if she did not get that, it is a legit complaint. You make that complaint to the city afterward, not with your bumper.

Missing work is bad. Driving into a crowd is worse.

text:
More Houston apartments are being sold by lenders and trustees instead of the owners who ran them. This month Price Per Door noted CBRE marketing two complexes for a Chapter 11 trustee, Colliers calling for offers on a 624-unit lender-owned portfolio, and a lender auction on a 441-unit property. CRED iQ puts Houston's CMBS distress rate at 15.3%, up from 12.4% a year earlier.

Buying from a lender is a different diligence job. Lenders usually sell as-is with few representations, and the people selling may have owned the property for only a short time. The T12 can mix months run by different managers, and the rent roll may not tell you who is actually paying.

So build the operating history yourself from bank deposits, utility bills, the work order log, open code issues and insurance claims, and expect the property to need more than the condition report shows.

The price can be right on these. You still need a reason your plan works where the last one didn't, like being local, buying at a lower basis or running tighter systems, and you should be able to say it in a sentence.

text:
This Week at Investing Angles — Part I: The Charts Have Started Talking Over Each Other

The Dollar keeps pushing, Europe has questions, bonds are making people uncomfortable, and several markets seem determined to test our sense of humor.

Another week, another impressive collection of charts trying to explain what is happening in the markets. Some old warnings have delivered almost exactly as expected, others are approaching important crossroads, and a few markets have apparently decided to change the script just when everyone was beginning to feel comfortable. It has been one of those weeks when you open a chart expecting a routine update and end up reconsidering the next several months.

The Dollar continues to flex its muscles, bonds are quietly making everyone nervous, and Gold and Silver are having their own disagreements with the bulls. Oil has reached an interesting destination, while equities are producing enough conflicting signals to keep us entertained well into next week. We also have two European studies, an uncomfortable Alphabet update, and a couple of free articles for readers who prefer to inspect the evidence before joining the caucus.

Welcome to Part I. The charts have plenty to say this week, and apparently nobody remembered to establish a speaking order.

CURRENCIES — THE DOLLAR HAS THE FLOOR

Dollar Index – Weekly Analysis

The Greenback is up roughly 4.5% since our September 11 bottom alert. Not a bad performance for a currency that was supposedly preparing for early retirement. Naturally, after such a rally, everyone wants to know whether the Dollar is getting tired or simply catching its breath before the next adventure. The latest weekly report revisits our larger roadmap and looks at several developments that could help answer that question. text:
In the twilight of empires and the dawn of the American experiment, the Founders stood at a crossroads of political thought. They sought to sever the ancient, unyielding chains of feudalism—where a human being was born as mere property to a crown, bound by an inescapable allegiance to soil and sovereign—and replace them with a republic forged by human will, reason, and the sacred architecture of consent.
To the architects of the early republic, citizenship was not an arbitrary chain; it was a covenant. Yet within this covenant lay two distinct pathways of belonging: one born of the organic pulse of the community itself, and the other crafted through the deliberate threshold of the law.

The Unconditional Root: The Natural-Born Citizen

To be natural-born is to enter the world already woven into the tapestry of the social compact. In the philosophical eye of the Founders, this status required no decree of a legislature, no stamp of a magistrate, and no probationary proving of one’s soul. It was an inheritance of belonging—an inherent tie to the political body established at the very first breath.
Because this citizenship sprang organically from the people themselves rather than as a gift from the state, the state could not place conditions upon its existence. What the government did not grant, the government could not withhold. It stood as an unconditioned truth: a child of the republic, tethered to its destiny not by statutory permission, but by native right.

The Conditional Threshold: The Naturalized Citizen

By contrast, the stranger arriving from distant shores stood outside the original circle of the compact. To invite that wanderer into the household of self-governance was an act of profound trust—a deliberate bridge built across the waters of past allegiances.
Because naturalization was an artificial creation of the law rather than a birthright of nature, it carried the weight of conditions. The republic asked the newcomer to pause at the threshold, to dwell among the people, to shed the titles and loyalties of old worlds, and to prove a harmony of spirit with the Constitution. Here, citizenship was a mutual vow: the individual offered a conscious, sworn devotion, and the sovereign people—through their laws—extended a conditional grace, welcoming a chosen kin into the fold.

The Guardian at the Gate

Nowhere was this philosophical divide more sharply etched than in the Founders’ vision of the presidency. Fearing the subtle poison of foreign intrigue and the divided heart of dual loyalties, they decreed that the highest steward of the nation must be one whose very origin lay within the American covenant. While the naturalized citizen was embraced as a full partner in the daily life of liberty, the pinnacle of executive power was reserved for one whose roots had never known another soil—a final safeguard to ensure the infant republic remained fiercely, undeniably its own.

text:
Prometheus Has a Problem: How Western Civilization Built the Modern World—and Nearly Destroyed It

From the mathematics of ancient Greece to the silicon chips powering artificial intelligence, Western civilization has transformed human existence. It has given the world extraordinary scientific discoveries, powerful institutions, remarkable wealth—and some of history’s greatest catastrophes. Now, as humanity approaches another technological revolution, an uncomfortable question emerges: Can a civilization become powerful enough to transform the world without becoming powerful enough to destroy it?

1. A Hole in the Roof—and a Mystery That Has Lasted 1,900 Years
Stand beneath the great dome of the Pantheon in Rome, and something extraordinary happens.
You look up.
High above, a perfect circular opening exposes the sky. Sunlight pours through it, moving slowly across the immense concrete ceiling as the Earth turns.
When rain falls, water enters the building. When the sun shines, a brilliant column of light illuminates the ancient interior.
There is no glass covering the opening.
No hidden steel skeleton holds up the dome.
And the structure has stood for almost nineteen centuries.
The present Pantheon was constructed during the reign of Emperor Hadrian, approximately AD 118–125. Its monumental concrete dome measures about 43.3 metres across and remains the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome.
Nearly two thousand years later, engineers still study how its builders managed the enormous forces involved.
Now imagine another scene.
It is the eighteenth century. An enslaved African lies in the crowded hold of a ship crossing the Atlantic. Thousands of miles away, merchants calculate profits, politicians discuss liberty, and European philosophers debate the natural rights of mankind.
Both scenes belong to the historical world we associate with Western civilization.
One represents humanity's extraordinary ability to understand and manipulate matter.
The other represents its terrifying ability to rationalize cruelty.
That contradiction lies at the centre of the Western story.
A short, visually spectacular video recently offered a different perspective. Beginning with Prometheus stealing fire from the gods, it raced through Euclid, Roman engineering, the Renaissance, oceanic exploration, steam power, the Hoover Dam and the microprocessor.
Its final destination was not Rome, London or Silicon Valley.
It was the stars.
The closing command consisted of a single word:
Accelerate.
It is an exhilarating vision of civilization as an unstoppable ascent toward technological mastery.
And yet history raises an awkward question.
What happens when humanity learns to build increasingly powerful machines faster than it learns to govern itself?
To answer that, we must examine not only what Western civilization achieved, but also how it achieved it, what it borrowed, whom it harmed, and why its greatest accomplishments remain inseparable from its deepest contradictions.

2. What Exactly Is Western Civilization? The Answer Is More Complicated Than a Map
Ask someone to identify Western civilization, and the usual answer begins with ancient Greece and Rome.
Then come Christianity, medieval Europe, the Renaissance, the Scientific Revolution, the Enlightenment, industrialization and modern democracy.
That sequence is familiar.
It is also deceptively tidy.
Ancient Greeks did not think of themselves as members of a civilization stretching toward modern America. The Roman Empire encompassed territories in Europe, North Africa and the Middle East. Christianity began in Roman-ruled Judea, not northern Europe.
The intellectual world of medieval Europe depended heavily on scholars working in Arabic, Persian, Greek, Hebrew and Latin.
And the modern idea of a unified "West" took shape through centuries of changing political, religious and cultural identities.
Western civilization is therefore not a single people, ethnicity or unbroken empire.
It is better understood as an evolving collection of institutions, intellectual traditions, technologies and cultural practices that developed primarily around the Mediterranean and Europe before spreading—sometimes voluntarily, sometimes violently—across much of the world.
Its defining characteristics have never been universally agreed upon.
Some emphasize Christianity and classical philosophy.
Others identify constitutional government, scientific inquiry, individual liberty or capitalism.
Still others argue that imperial expansion and racial hierarchy must be recognized as central to its historical development rather than treated as unfortunate exceptions.
Each interpretation highlights something real.
None fully captures the whole.
The most productive question is not whether every Western society possessed a particular virtue.
It is how certain ideas and institutions became unusually influential, why they spread, and why their consequences were so uneven.
One especially consequential inheritance was the belief that claims about the world could be subjected to systematic criticism.
That brings us to a Greek mathematician whose influence was arguably greater than that of many emperors.

3. Euclid's Dangerous Idea: Even the Greatest Authority Must Offer Proof
Around 300 BC, in the intellectual world of Alexandria, a mathematician known as Euclid compiled a work that would shape scientific reasoning for more than two millennia.
Its title was deceptively ordinary:
Elements.
The revolutionary idea was not simply geometry.
People had measured land, calculated areas and studied numerical relationships long before Euclid. Babylonian and Egyptian mathematicians possessed substantial practical knowledge.
Euclid's achievement was the systematic organization of mathematical propositions through definitions, assumptions and logical demonstrations.
Begin with accepted premises.
Proceed through justified steps.
Reach a conclusion.
In this intellectual framework, a proposition is not true merely because a respected authority announces it.
It must follow from an argument that others can examine.
The principle sounds obvious today.
It was not always obvious in human societies organized around inherited status, sacred tradition and political authority.
Of course, mathematical proof is not the same as political freedom. Ancient Greek societies remained hierarchical, and their philosophers disagreed profoundly about democracy.
Nevertheless, the habits encouraged by deductive reasoning proved remarkably transferable.
A bridge must stand because its design satisfies physical requirements, not because its architect has powerful friends.
A scientific hypothesis must confront evidence.
A computer program must produce consistent results.
A legal judgment ought to rest on defensible reasoning rather than personal whim.
Euclid did not invent modern science, constitutional government or software engineering.
But the mathematical tradition associated with his work helped establish one of civilization's most powerful intellectual disciplines:
A claim should be capable of surviving questions.
The great irony is that societies celebrating this principle have repeatedly tried to exempt their own political or religious authorities from it.
The struggle between evidence and power has never ended.

4. Rome's Greatest Invention Was Not Concrete. It Was Continuity.
The Romans left roads, aqueducts, bridges, amphitheatres and cities.
They developed sophisticated legal and administrative practices that influenced later European institutions.
But their remarkable achievement was not merely knowing how to construct things.
It was organizing people, materials, labour and authority across vast distances.
Consider the Pantheon.
Its dome required more than ingenious concrete.
It required the ability to obtain building materials, coordinate skilled workers, construct massive foundations and sustain a large project over time.
Roman engineers also understood that concrete mixtures and aggregate choices affected structural weight.
The Pantheon's enormous walls support a dome whose design becomes progressively lighter toward the top.
Its celebrated oculus is both an architectural feature and a reduction in the load carried by the structure.
Yet Rome's administrative power had a darker foundation.
The empire expanded through conquest, taxed conquered populations and made extensive use of enslaved labour.
Its legal system distinguished sharply among citizens, non-citizens, freed persons and enslaved people.
Roman citizenship eventually expanded, but legal equality in the modern sense did not exist.
The same institutional capacity that maintained roads could also provision armies and enforce imperial domination.
This is a recurring historical pattern.
Large organizations can accomplish extraordinary things.
But efficiency does not tell us whether their objectives are just.
A well-organized hospital and a well-organized prison may both demonstrate impressive administrative competence.
Civilization must be judged partly by what its institutions are designed to achieve.
Rome also teaches another lesson: technological sophistication does not guarantee political survival.
The western Roman imperial government collapsed in the fifth century, even though many of its material and institutional traditions endured.
Its eastern continuation, now commonly called the Byzantine Empire, survived for nearly another thousand years.
Knowledge, institutions and identities can outlive states.
That capacity for transmission would become crucial to Europe's later development.

5. The Renaissance Was Not Europe's Solo Performance
There is a popular story about the Renaissance.
After centuries of intellectual darkness, Europeans rediscovered ancient Greece, remembered how to think, and began inventing the modern world.
The actual history is more interesting.
Classical knowledge never disappeared completely from Europe. Byzantine scholars preserved Greek traditions, while monasteries and other institutions maintained substantial bodies of Latin learning.
Meanwhile, intellectual centres across the Islamic world translated, studied, criticized and expanded upon Greek scientific and philosophical works.
Scholars writing in Arabic developed mathematics, medicine, optics, astronomy and philosophy.
The mathematical tradition associated with al-Khwarizmi contributed to the development of algebra and the transmission of numerical techniques.
The decimal positional numeral system, developed through Indian mathematical traditions, spread through the Islamic world and eventually transformed European calculation.
Chinese innovations in papermaking, printing, gunpowder and navigation travelled through complex networks of exchange.
UNESCO's research on the Silk Roads emphasizes precisely this point: trade routes carried not just silk and spices, but scientific knowledge, technologies, religious ideas and artistic traditions.
The movement was rarely simple.
Ideas were translated, modified, misunderstood, improved and sometimes independently rediscovered.
This does not diminish Europe's later achievements.
It explains how intellectual progress actually works.
Civilizations are not sealed laboratories.
They are participants in a vast conversation.
Consider the construction of Florence Cathedral's celebrated dome.
In 1420, Filippo Brunelleschi confronted an architectural problem that had frustrated Florentine builders for generations.
The cathedral had an enormous opening above its central space.
How could anyone cover it without constructing an immense wooden supporting framework?
Brunelleschi developed an ingenious system involving a double-shell structure, carefully organized brickwork and innovative lifting machinery.
Construction continued until 1436.
The result remains one of the Renaissance's greatest engineering achievements.
But Brunelleschi did not create his methods out of nothing.
He studied ancient architecture, including Roman achievements, while working within a wealthy commercial city supported by skilled artisans, technical knowledge and ambitious patrons.
Behind the apparent miracle stood centuries of accumulated experience.
Genius matters. But genius becomes transformative when knowledge, tools, resources and opportunity meet.
The same principle will reappear centuries later in an unlikely partnership between a Japanese calculator company and a young American semiconductor manufacturer.

6. Magellan's Great Voyage: The Man Who Did Not Finish the Journey That Made Him Famous
In September 1519, a fleet of five ships departed Spain under the command of Ferdinand Magellan, a Portuguese navigator serving the Spanish Crown.
Its objective was commercial.
The expedition sought a westward route to the valuable spice-producing regions of Asia.
The journey became one of the most consequential voyages in maritime history.
The expedition passed through the southern tip of South America, crossed the Pacific Ocean and reached the Philippines.
But Magellan never returned to Europe.
He was killed in the Philippines in 1521, during fighting on Mactan.
The voyage was completed under Juan Sebastián Elcano.
When the Victoria returned to Spain in September 1522, only eighteen men from the returning ship had survived the entire journey.
The expedition achieved the first documented circumnavigation of the globe by a ship.
It did not prove that Earth was round. Educated people had known Earth's spherical shape long before 1519.
Instead, it demonstrated the extraordinary navigational and logistical possibility of completing a global circuit.
The voyage also illustrates how the language of discovery can obscure the experience of those who were supposedly "discovered."
The peoples of the Pacific and Indian Ocean had developed sophisticated maritime knowledge long before Europeans arrived.
European navigation depended at various points on local pilots, regional expertise and existing trade networks.
The new oceanic routes increasingly connected distant economies.
They also facilitated conquest, missionary expansion, forced labour, disease transmission and the growth of colonial empires.
For European merchants, the oceans became highways of opportunity.
For many Indigenous communities, those same highways brought dispossession and catastrophe.
The ships carried both maps and weapons.
We should not pretend that one cancels the other.

7. Why Did Europe Become So Rich? Historians Are Still Fighting Over the Answer
For most of human history, sustained increases in average living standards were relatively limited.
Societies could become wealthier for a time, but population growth, warfare, disease and other pressures often consumed their gains.
Then, beginning with industrialization, parts of the world experienced a dramatic and eventually sustained rise in productivity.
This transformation is frequently called the Great Enrichment.
But why did it begin in Britain and parts of northwestern Europe?
Why not in China, India or the Ottoman Empire?
The question has occupied generations of economic historians.
One influential explanation emphasizes institutions and intellectual culture.
Europe contained competing states, universities, commercial networks, scientific societies and communities of scholars who exchanged discoveries across political boundaries.
Political fragmentation sometimes encouraged persecution and warfare. It could also allow dissident thinkers, skilled workers and entrepreneurs to move elsewhere.
In 1660, England's Royal Society emerged from gatherings devoted to natural philosophy.
Its members conducted experiments, exchanged observations and eventually published their findings.
Over time, increasingly organized scientific communities helped transform isolated discoveries into cumulative knowledge.
Another explanation emphasizes natural resources and economic incentives.
Britain possessed accessible coal deposits.
In certain industries, relatively expensive labour made labour-saving machinery commercially attractive.
Overseas colonies supplied materials, markets and profits.
Historian Kenneth Pomeranz famously emphasized the importance of coal and access to resources from the Americas in explaining the divergence between European and Asian economic development.
Joel Mokyr, by contrast, has placed considerable emphasis on useful knowledge, intellectual openness and institutions that encouraged technological innovation.
Other scholars emphasize wages, energy prices, state capacity, colonial extraction, agricultural change or combinations of these factors.
The debate remains active because no single explanation accounts for every region, period and industry.
Then came a striking development in October 2025.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences awarded the Economics Prize to Joel Mokyr, Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt for explaining innovation-driven economic growth.
Mokyr was recognized for investigating the conditions that allowed technological progress to become sustained.
Aghion and Howitt were honoured for their theory of growth through creative destruction.
Their work addresses a deceptively simple question:
Why do some societies experience one invention after another, while others fail to turn discoveries into lasting prosperity?
Consider James Watt.
Watt did not invent the steam engine.
Earlier engineers, including Thomas Newcomen, had already developed working engines.
Watt's major contribution was improving their efficiency, particularly through the separate condenser patented in 1769.
The Science Museum in London notes that this innovation could reduce coal consumption by roughly two-thirds compared with earlier designs.
That improvement helped make steam power economically useful across more settings.
Factories could expand.
Mines could operate more effectively.
Production increasingly escaped the limitations of human and animal muscle.
The steam engine was not merely a machine.
It was a new way of organizing economic life.
Factories created extraordinary productive capacity, but also concentrated workers, capital and industrial pollution.
New industries displaced older occupations.
Some people accumulated fortunes while others endured dangerous workplaces and exhausting labour.
This is creative destruction in its rawest historical form.
Progress creates opportunities.
It also creates casualties.
The question is whether society possesses the institutions needed to share its benefits and reduce its costs.

8. The Atlantic Slave Trade: Civilization's Most Uncomfortable Balance Sheet
Numbers can sometimes describe a historical tragedy more clearly than rhetoric.
According to the SlaveVoyages research project, approximately 12.5 million enslaved Africans were forced aboard ships participating in the transatlantic slave trade.
About 10.7 million survived the Atlantic crossing.
The difference represents roughly 1.8 million people who did not survive the voyage, although estimates remain subject to historical uncertainty.
Those numbers do not capture the full human cost.
They exclude many deaths associated with capture, forced marches, confinement and violence before embarkation, as well as suffering after arrival.
The people involved were not anonymous units of labour.
They were children, parents, farmers, craftspeople, merchants and members of communities whose lives were violently disrupted.
European merchants and colonial powers played central roles in organizing and profiting from the trade.
Some African rulers, merchants and intermediaries also participated in supplying captives.
Recognizing their involvement does not remove responsibility from the Atlantic powers that created and sustained enormous markets for enslaved labour.
Plantation economies generated wealth through sugar, tobacco, cotton and other commodities.
That wealth was intertwined with European and American commercial development.
Exactly how much slavery and colonial extraction contributed to industrialization remains debated.
Some economic historians consider their contribution indispensable to the rise of Western wealth.
Others argue that domestic productivity, technological change and European institutions would have supported substantial growth even without colonial empires.
These are disagreements about historical causation, not about whether enslavement was a profound human wrong.
Yet the story contains another contradiction.
Western political thought increasingly developed languages of liberty, legal equality and universal rights.
The American Declaration of Independence proclaimed human equality in 1776, while slavery remained entrenched in American society.
The French Revolution declared the rights of man in 1789, but women were not granted equal political participation.
In 1791, Olympe de Gouges published her Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen, challenging the exclusion of women.
She was executed in 1793 during the revolutionary Terror, following political conflict and prosecution.
The contradiction between universal principles and selective application became impossible to ignore.
And some of the most decisive challenges came from people whom European political systems had excluded.
Beginning in 1791, enslaved people in the French colony of Saint-Domingue rose in a revolutionary struggle.
In 1804, Haiti became independent.
The Haitian Revolution demonstrated that enslaved people were not merely passive beneficiaries of European abolitionist ideas.
They were political actors who fought for their own freedom.
The struggle against slavery included African resistance, Caribbean revolutions, religious movements, political organizing and antislavery campaigns across many societies.
This is one of history's most important lessons:
A civilization's ideals can be greater than the people who first proclaim them.
Those excluded from the original promise may become the very people who force it toward fulfillment.

9. The Great Paradox of Western Liberty: Rights Were Often Won Against Western Power
Modern constitutional government did not appear fully formed in ancient Athens.
It developed through centuries of political conflict.
The Magna Carta of 1215 was initially a settlement between King John and rebellious English barons.
It was not a declaration of universal human equality.
Nevertheless, its later legal and political interpretation helped reinforce the principle that rulers could be constrained by law.
Representative institutions gradually expanded.
Religious conflicts encouraged arguments about toleration.
The Enlightenment challenged inherited authority.
Constitutional revolutions established new ideas of citizenship, representation and legitimate government.
But none of these developments followed a straight line.
Ancient Athenian democracy excluded women, enslaved people and many residents from political participation.
European monarchies resisted parliamentary limits.
Revolutionary governments sometimes suppressed dissent in the name of liberty.
Industrial societies took generations to extend voting rights to large parts of their populations.
The right to vote, organize, publish and criticize governments often had to be won through sustained struggle.
There is a powerful distinction here.
A society may celebrate freedom as an ideal while denying it in practice.
The real measure of its commitment is whether excluded people can challenge that contradiction without being silenced.
Democracy also requires more than elections.
A government elected by popular vote can still attempt to undermine courts, intimidate journalists or weaken opposition parties.
Constitutional democracy depends on enforceable rules that limit what winners may do to losers.
In a 1947 parliamentary debate, Winston Churchill repeated the famous observation that democracy was the worst form of government, except the other forms that had been tried.
The remark is often treated as a joke.
Its deeper point concerns political humility.
No government possesses perfect wisdom.
Therefore, citizens need institutions capable of detecting mistakes, challenging authority and replacing leaders without civil war.
This may be Western political thought's most valuable practical insight:
A good political system should not require good rulers all the time. It should contain safeguards for when rulers are mistaken, incompetent or corrupt.

text:
The Parable of the Vaccine from the Stars

As told by Professor Eleanor Whitcombe, Harvard Business School, to a room of first-year MBAs

Let me tell you a story. It's apocryphal, mostly, but I've found it lands better than any case study I've ever assigned.

One gray Tuesday morning, a silver vessel the size of a small city settled over the Atlantic. The aliens who emerged were tall, soft-spoken, and, as it turned out, extremely patient. Their message was simple: We have a vaccine. It will end your most persistent diseases. We would like to give it to you.

Well, you can imagine. The world convened immediately.

The scientists went first. A virologist from Geneva asked about the mechanism of action. The aliens answered at length, with diagrams that made three Nobel laureates quietly sit down. An epidemiologist asked about trial design. "We have run it across eleven thousand worlds," said the aliens. "Does that suffice?" It did not, entirely, but it was a start.

The safety people came next. Regulators asked about long-term side effects, about interactions with existing medications, about pregnant women and children and the immunocompromised. The aliens answered every question, patiently, and offered to repeat any answer in any language we preferred.

The ethicists asked about consent and equity. The engineers asked about storage and distribution. A senator asked, "What's in it for you?" and the aliens replied, "The pleasure of seeing you flourish." The senator wrote that down and underlined it twice, the way people do when they don't believe something.

For weeks this went on. Thousands of questions. Millions of pages of transcripts. Every expert had their turn, and every answer came back clear, thorough, and, frustratingly, satisfactory.

And then, one afternoon, a woman named Linda stood up. Linda ran a mid-sized logistics company in Ohio. She wasn't a scientist or a diplomat. She had a lanyard, a lukewarm coffee, and a reputation for never leaving a table without something extra.

She looked at the aliens for a long moment, and the room went quiet.

"This is all very impressive," Linda said. "But I have to ask..."

(Here Professor Whitcombe pauses, smiles, and a glint appears in her eye.)

"...Can we negotiate a better deal?"

The aliens, I'm told, blinked slowly. Then, for the first time in the whole encounter, they laughed, a sound like wind chimes in a thunderstorm. "Finally," said the lead alien. "Someone asked. Eleven thousand worlds, and only a handful ever do."

They threw in free distribution logistics, a booster at no charge, and a lifetime supply of a very nice tea.

Linda, of course, got a finder's fee.

(Professor Whitcombe taps the lectern.)

So here's what I want you to remember: you can ask every smart question in the world, and still miss the one that matters. Expertise tells you what's true. Negotiation tells you what's possible. Never accept the first offer, even if it comes from the stars. 😁

Class dismissed.

don't get me wrong; i'm a paper ballot & hand counting guy

the machines are selected at the state or county level and there are several vendors for them. problems found with one of those vendors or installations don't necessarily extend to the others.

saying that there's a national problem with voting machines is an extremely bold claim to be making and absolutely *requires* physical evidence. it'd only be possible with cooperation among the manufacturers, at the very, very least. it'd probably also require the involvement of people in the precincts where the corrupted machines were used.

i'm not saying it's not possible. i'm saying it's a really big thing to be suggesting and those kinds of suggestions create problems if they're offered without any evidence. it's the sort of thing you need to figure out and dig up the details on before going public with it.

on machines generally, there are two problems which create a catch 22 situation.

first, they have to be open source. not just software, but the hardware, too. we, the people must be able to inspect our election systems in their entirety. not just the election processes, but the equipment itself. 

anything less will always result in questions about the result, regardless of who wins. this has been the case since democrats first challenged the diebold machines in ohio.

second, they can't be open source. especially now, in the emerging age of ai hacking. open source hw/sw provides motivated, resourceful people with the ability to find flaws that others don't know about and thus can't be fixed.

the only solution to the machine problem is to get rid of the machines. but i don't see any evidence that there's a nationwide voting machine fraud issue, either, unless you have something new to share.

$NVDA NVIDIA EARNINGS, TUESDAY NOVEMBER 17: THE COMPLETE DILIGENCE LIST

THE SETUP

Nvidia reports fiscal Q3 after the close on Tuesday, November 17. The quarter ended October 25. Guidance is revenue of $108 billion plus or minus 2 percent, gross margin 74 percent plus or minus 50 basis points. Consensus sits at $109.0 billion for revenue and $2.47 for adjusted earnings per share, and it has barely moved in four weeks. The street has not cut this quarter for the governance crisis. The numbers it expects are the numbers the old regime promised.

This is also the first print of the post-Jensen era. Colette Kress runs the call as interim CEO and CFO. The numbers matter. The language matters more. Here is everything worth monitoring, in the order it will arrive.

THE NUMBERS, FIRST 10 MINUTES

- Revenue against the $108 billion guide and the $109.0 billion consensus. A print inside the guide band but below consensus is a miss wearing a beat's clothes. Score it as a miss.
- Data center revenue against $101.8 billion of consensus, and inside it compute against $80.7 billion and networking against $20.0 billion. Networking strong with compute light is mix shift toward systems. Both light is a demand problem.
- The segment cuts by customer type: hyperscale at $53.3 billion of consensus, AI clouds and industrial at $48.9 billion, edge computing at $7.5 billion. The AI clouds line is the neocloud bucket. Its beat or miss is the cleanest read on the demand quality of the ecosystem Nvidia finances.
- Gross margin against the 74 percent guide and 74.1 percent consensus. Last quarter guided the fiscal Q4 margin down to a 71 to 72 percent trough, partly on memory costs. Slippage now means the trough arrives early or deeper.
- Operating discipline: consensus expects $72.1 billion of adjusted operating income on $9.0 billion of operating expense. In a transition quarter, expense discipline is the first place a careful CFO shows her hand.
- Everything outside data center is only about $7 billion of the $109 billion. Gaming, visualization, and autos cannot save a data center miss or sink a data center beat. Note them and move on.
- Free cash flow against roughly $59 billion of consensus, and the quarter's buyback total. Acceleration reads as management buying its own transition discount. Deceleration reads as conservation ahead of the commitment stack.
- Inventory, receivables, and days sales outstanding. In a quarter defined by a diversion scandal running through intermediaries, receivables growing faster than revenue is the first number skeptics will reach for.
- Operating cash flow against net income. The quality test that has flagged lesser names all season.

THE GUIDE

The Q4 guide is the only forward number that matters Tuesday night. Consensus for Q4 already sits at $124.7 billion of revenue, with the margin trough of about 71.9 percent built in. The lowest published model, already cut once for export restriction risk, is $120 billion. A guide that reaches only the low model is a consensus miss of nearly $5 billion, and it will be traded as one.

More important than the guide itself is one sentence from last quarter. On the August call, management guided preliminary fiscal 2028 revenue growth of approximately 70 percent year over year, supply constrained. Reaffirmed, qualified, or silently dropped are three different stocks. That sentence gets compared word by word against the August transcript.

Watch also for any new caveat vocabulary that was not there in August: visibility, prudence, transition. New words in a guidance paragraph are a downgrade in plain sight.

PRODUCT AND SUPPLY

- Vera Rubin was guided to about 20 percent of Q3 data center revenue. Above or below that line grades the ramp.
- Supply and capacity commitments went from $119 billion to $279 billion in a single quarter, mostly memory procurement. The new 10-Q figure is a same-night check. Another step up of that size is demand conviction and balance sheet commitment in the same number.
- Memory pricing. Management's own flagged line last quarter was that the magnitude of the price increase had exceeded expectations. Whether HBM costs are still escalating, now locked, or passing through to prices decides the margin path into 2027.
- Any cancellation, pushout, or double-ordering language, anywhere on the call.

CHINA AND EXPORT CONTROLS

The standing line is no China data center compute revenue in the outlook. Unchanged, loosened, or tightened all trade differently.

Nobody will say the words Megaspeed or diversion. Listen instead for the euphemisms: certain customers, enhanced know-your-customer, end-use verification, new compliance costs. And in the 10-Q, watch the revenue geography note. Last quarter's filing reclassified $20.6 billion of Singapore-billed revenue by buyer headquarters, $5.35 billion of it to China and Hong Kong. Whether that presentation extends or quietly disappears is a disclosure decision, and it will be read as one.

If an analyst forces a revenue-at-risk number for the export bills now moving in Congress, whether management quantifies or refuses is itself the tell.

THE ECOSYSTEM BALANCE SHEET

Nvidia is the AI ecosystem's underwriter as well as its supplier, and the call is a chance to see whether that changes. The stack to re-read in the new 10-Q: $279 billion of supply commitments, $36 billion of AI cloud purchase agreements, $108.5 billion of maximum guarantee exposure including $105 billion of residual value guarantees behind a single Ohio campus leased to OpenAI, about $164.5 billion of total customer support against $229 billion of shareholders' equity.

Listen for whether the August financing platforms with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR get mentioned at all, and in what tense: expanding, continuing, or under review. Listen for any pacing, discipline, or review language around new partner support. And listen for neocloud credit quality and customer concentration, the transmission channel through which a leadership transition reaches the rest of the complex.

GOVERNANCE AND LEADERSHIP

The board said on November 13 that it is selecting a search firm and has not formally engaged any candidate. On the call: is a firm named, are criteria stated, is a timeline offered or refused, and do the stated criteria echo the congressional chairs' demand for leadership that makes national security the top priority.

Watch Kress's register. Operator language is decisions, allocations, timelines. Caretaker language is continuity, stability, process. The market will grade the difference even if no one says so.

Watch for any reference to Huang, any update on the board's November 8 independent investigation, and any severance, equity, or clawback terms that the November 12 filing did not disclose. And watch the analysts: who asks the first succession question, and how many follow, tells you whether the street is treating this as a fundamentals print or a governance print.

One more piece of context: this call is management's last scheduled public appearance before the December congressional calendar, the interview deadline, the Teter session, and the public hearing. Any question about Congress gets a decline. The decline is free. Anything beyond it is news.

IN THE 10-Q, AFTER THE CALL

- How the November 9 securities class action is described, and whether any accrual appears.
- Any new disclosure of a government inquiry, subpoena, or investigation.
- The subsequent events note, and risk factor changes against last quarter, read word by word.
- The legal proceedings and commitments notes are the only places the insurance and indemnification story can surface. Check them. Expect nothing. Be surprised correctly if there is something.

THE QUESTIONS THAT MATTER

1. Does the preliminary fiscal 2028 growth expectation of about 70 percent still stand?
2. Where do supply commitments stand now, and how much is memory?
3. Is any China data center revenue in the Q4 outlook, and what is the status of H200 licensing?
4. What revenue is exposed to the remote access and chip security legislation?
5. What has changed in end-use verification for cloud partners in the last 90 days?
6. What is the current total of guarantees and partner support, and is the board reviewing the pace?
7. The August financing platforms: expanding, continuing, or under review?
8. CEO search: firm, criteria, timeline?
9. Any severance, equity, or clawback arrangements with Mr. Huang beyond what has been filed?
10. Any inquiry or subpoena from the Commerce Department, the Justice Department, or the SEC on export compliance?
11. Status and expected timeline of the board's November 8 investigation?
12. Is the 71 to 72 percent margin trough still the fiscal Q4 expectation, and what drives the recovery after it?
13. How much of the quarter, and of the guide, is sovereign AI demand, the category most exposed to the export rule fight and the one management has always liked to showcase?

READING THE OUTCOMES

Clean print, guide at the bogey, the 2028 language intact, operator tone: the institution is bigger than the man, and the market starts pricing the successor's Nvidia instead of the founder's absence.

Soft guide or qualified language: the transition tax is real and gets priced over quarters, not days.

A hard guide down or caretaker tone: the print stops being about the quarter at all, and every open question, the search, the investigation, the legislation, the litigation, reprices at once.

The founder is gone. Tuesday night is the first evidence of what exactly left with him.

text:
$NVDA $MU $SNDK $LITE WHAT HAPPENS TO THE $500B CONSORTIUM

Short answer: it does not unwind. It decelerates, it gets more expensive, and it gets governed. The headline number was a Jensen number. The capital is not.

Start with what the consortium actually is. The August platforms with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR are independent financing vehicles meant to mobilize over $500B of third-party capital into AI compute infrastructure. Mobilize is the operative word. $500B was never wired. It was a target that depended on a continuous flow of new deals, and the flow depended on one man standing in the middle of it.

The committed capital stays. Those six firms are not charities and they are not Jensen's friends. They are asset managers whose economics run on infrastructure cash flows, contracted offtake, and GPU collateral that has held its value. LP money does not get recalled because a CEO resigns, and performing vehicles keep funding. Anyone predicting the consortium collapses is wrong.

What dies is the origination, and origination was the whole story. The platforms were underwritable at that scale because Nvidia supplied three things no contract fully captured: demand visibility years out, allocation priority for the vehicles' projects, and the implicit assurance that the ecosystem's central bank would keep the music playing. All three were personal to Jensen. He was the Bank of Nvidia. An interim CFO and a board under a securities class action cannot reissue that assurance, and would not if they could.

So expect three changes.

First, velocity. No new headline platforms get announced while the CEO seat is empty, and deal approvals that used to take a phone call now take a committee. The machine keeps running. It just runs at institutional speed instead of Jensen speed.

Second, terms. Without the implicit backstop, the sponsors reprice. The marginal buyer of compute, the neoclouds and the second tier data center developers, pays more for capital or does not get it. We already have an early data point: this week QTS cut a planned private debt sale from roughly $800M to roughly $300M. That is the financing channel repricing in real time, before any headline forces it.

Third, governance. A board defending a securities lawsuit does not expand the one structure every critic already calls circular vendor financing. Expect a quiet review of the platforms, tighter disclosure, more distance between Nvidia and the vehicles, and a permanent CEO who treats the whole apparatus as a liability to be managed rather than an empire to be extended.

Layer on the regulatory side and it tightens further. A meaningful share of what these platforms fund is neocloud and overseas capacity, which is precisely what the remote access bills and chip tracking proposals are aimed at. Sponsors price that cliff whether or not the bills pass this session.

The tells to watch: whether Kress mentions the financing partnerships on Tuesday's call, whether any of the six partners publicly reaffirms while the seat is empty, whether a platform lapses without a successor, and whether the next CEO keeps the financing function at Jensen's scale or folds it into ordinary treasury discipline.

Your label is right about the origination. It was a mafia in the structural sense: loyalty and flow organized around one man. But the money is institutional, and institutional money does not leave. It just stops moving fast. What Jensen built in a phone call, his successors will administer in a process. The $500B was the process running at his speed. At theirs, it is a smaller, slower, more expensive machine, and the difference between those two numbers is the real size of the man.

Go behind the scenes as John Cena says goodbye.

By Christopher Hudspeth

June 23, 2026

WWE Unreal is making its return with a fresh batch of behind-the-scenes action in Season 3.

After taking fans deeper than ever inside World Wrestling Entertainment’s creative process, the hit docuseries will once again pull back the curtain on some of the biggest moments, boldest decisions, and unforgettable storytelling with some of the WWE’s greatest legends who’ve shaped the industry and new stars who are emerging as prominent parts of the future.

What will be shown in WWE Unreal Season 3?

In WWE Unreal Season 3, John Cena says goodbye, a fan favorite returns, and the next generation of Superstars rise to the occasion.

The series takes viewers inside the writers room as injuries, last-minute pivots, and career-defining decisions reshape WWE’s biggest season yet heading into WrestleMania 42.

Who will be featured in WWE Unreal Season 3?

The cast of WWE Superstars featured in WWE Unreal Season 3 includes John Cena, Cody Rhodes, Liv Morgan, CM Punk, AJ Lee, Trick Williams, Lash Legend, Stephanie Vaquer, Oba Femi, Bron Breakker, Chelsea Green, Matt Cardona, Seth Rollins, and Becky Lynch.

When does WWE Unreal Season 3 come out?

WWE Unreal Season 3 will be released on July 21.

How many episodes are in WWE Unreal Season 3?

WWE Unreal Season 3 will have five 50-minute episodes.

Here's the latest Netflix news as of mid-January 2026!

The streaming giant is kicking off the year strong with a packed slate of new releases, ongoing buzz around major deals, and continued subscriber growth.

Major Highlights

Netflix is reportedly in the midst of a blockbuster acquisition: the company has agreed to buy Warner Bros. in a massive deal valued at around $82.7 billion (with some reports citing $72 billion in equity value).

This move aims to supercharge its content library with iconic franchises like Harry Potter and classic films.

However, there's drama — Paramount Skydance has launched a competing hostile takeover bid for Warner Bros. Discovery, adding some high-stakes industry intrigue!

Netflix ended 2025 with over 301.6 million global subscribers, solidifying its position as the top streaming platform.

What's New & Coming in January 2026

January is loaded with fresh originals, from thrilling mysteries to romantic adaptations and long-awaited returns.

Here are some of the standout releases that are lighting up the charts and generating buzz right now:

People We Meet on Vacation — A charming rom-com adaptation of the Emily Henry novel, starring Emily Bader — it's been topping the charts as one of the biggest new movies of the year so far!

The Rip — This high-octane action-thriller directed by Joe Carnahan reunites Ben Affleck and Matt Damon — it's one of the most anticipated films dropping mid-month, perfect for fans of intense heist vibes!

His & Hers — A gripping mystery series starring Tessa Thompson and Jon Bernthal, following estranged spouses racing to solve a murder. It's been climbing the Top 10 with strong buzz around its twists.

Bridgerton Season 4 — The Regency-era drama returns later in the month (Part 1 premiering around Jan 29), with plenty of masquerade glamour and romance — the premiere events are already making waves!

Other notables include:

Kidnapped: Elizabeth Smart (true-crime docuseries)

New seasons of hits like Unlocked: A Jail Experiment, Love Is Blind: Germany, and WWE Unreal

Stand-up specials and reality shows keeping the variety flowing.

Plus, don't miss the Stranger Things 5 making-of documentary One Last Adventure, which premiered earlier this month for fans wanting a deep dive into the finale. Netflix is clearly doubling down on big stars, book adaptations, and high-energy originals to keep viewers hooked in 2026. (Grok)

Netflix is a global streaming service providing a vast library of films, TV shows, documentaries, and mobile games. As of 2026, it has approximately 325 million paid members across more than 190 countries.

Pricing & Plans: Subscription plans typically range from $7.99 to $24.99 per month.

Content Offerings: Includes "Netflix Originals" (like Stranger Things and Squid Game), licensed content, and a growing selection of live programming and video podcasts.

Device Compatibility: Streamable on smart TVs, game consoles, smartphones, tablets, and via https://t.co/YlumK0CxOt.

Features: Supports offline downloads, personalized recommendations, and a dedicated "Netflix Kids" experience with parental controls.

Recent 2026 Developments

Warner Bros. Merger News: As of January 21, 2026, Netflix has moved toward an all-cash $27.75-per-share offer to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery, aiming to outbid Paramount.

Market Reaction: Despite a Q4 earnings beat, Netflix shares saw a 7% decline in some markets (e.g., Frankfurt) on January 21, 2026, due to investor concerns regarding the financial weight of the Warner Bros. acquisition.

New Initiatives: The company is expanding into vertical video features for mobile and has recently launched video podcasts.

Live Events: Upcoming live events include the world-record climber Alex Honnold's "Skyscraper Live" ascent of Taipei 101 on January 23, 2026.

WWE Unreal

WWE Unreal is a professional wrestling documentary and reality series on Netflix that provides an unprecedented behind-the-scenes look at the creative process and internal operations of WWE.

WWE Unreal

Show Overview

Genre: Reality television / Documentary series.

Premise: The series follows WWE Superstars and executives, notably Paul "Triple H" Levesque, as they plan storylines in the writers' room and manage the "Gorilla Position" during live broadcasts.

Production: A collaboration between WWE, Omaha Productions (Peyton Manning), NFL Films, and Skydance Sports.

Seasons & Episodes

The series has released two seasons as of January 2026:

Season 1: Premiered July 29, 2025. It chronicled the lead-up to the debut of WWE Raw on Netflix and WrestleMania 41. Notable segments included a look at John Cena's high-profile storyline turns and the return of Charlotte Flair.

Season 2: Released January 20, 2026. This five-episode season focuses on the "Road to SummerSlam 2025" and features superstars like Seth Rollins, Becky Lynch, Rhea Ripley, and Cody Rhodes.

It delves into real-life drama such as R-Truth's contract negotiations and Naomi's previous walkout from the company.

Season 3: Confirmed to be in development, expected to focus on John Cena's retirement tour.

Key Personalities Featured

Executives: Paul "Triple H" Levesque (Narrator), Peyton Manning (Executive Producer).

Superstars: John Cena, Roman Reigns, Cody Rhodes, CM Punk, Rhea Ripley, Becky Lynch, Seth Rollins, and Bianca Belair.

Action Figures: Mattel has released sets like the "Hall of Champions" 4-pack featuring legendary superstars seen in the series.

WWE Unreal

WWE Unreal is a professional wrestling documentary and reality series on Netflix that provides an unprecedented behind-the-scenes look at the creative process and internal operations of WWE.

WWE Unreal

Show Overview

Genre: Reality television / Documentary series.

Premise: The series follows WWE Superstars and executives, notably Paul "Triple H" Levesque, as they plan storylines in the writers' room and manage the "Gorilla Position" during live broadcasts.

Production: A collaboration between WWE, Omaha Productions (Peyton Manning), NFL Films, and Skydance Sports.

Seasons & Episodes

The series has released two seasons as of January 2026:

Season 1: Premiered July 29, 2025. It chronicled the lead-up to the debut of WWE Raw on Netflix and WrestleMania 41. Notable segments included a look at John Cena's high-profile storyline turns and the return of Charlotte Flair.

Season 2: Released January 20, 2026. This five-episode season focuses on the "Road to SummerSlam 2025" and features superstars like Seth Rollins, Becky Lynch, Rhea Ripley, and Cody Rhodes.

It delves into real-life drama such as R-Truth's contract negotiations and Naomi's previous walkout from the company.

Season 3: Confirmed to be in development, expected to focus on John Cena's retirement tour.

Key Personalities Featured

Executives: Paul "Triple H" Levesque (Narrator), Peyton Manning (Executive Producer).

Superstars: John Cena, Roman Reigns, Cody Rhodes, CM Punk, Rhea Ripley, Becky Lynch, Seth Rollins, and Bianca Belair.

text:
#DidYouKnow that Pushmataha raised a company of Choctaw warriors to support American forces during the War of 1812? After refusing to join Tecumseh’s confederacy at the start of the war, the Choctaw remained neutral until August 1813. When the Red Stick Creeks attacked Fort Mims, Pushmataha approached Brig. Gen. Thomas Flournoy and offered his support. He was commissioned as a captain, and eventually lieutenant colonel, and went on to raise a battalion that fought at the Battle of Holy Ground on December 23, 1813. In early 1814, his warriors skirmished with the Red Sticks around the Tombigbee and Black Warrior Rivers before helping the Americans emerge victorious at the Battle of Horseshoe Bend. For his service, Pushmataha was promoted to brigadier general. Some of his warriors later supported General Andrew Jackson at the Battle of New Orleans before returning to Mississippi. #NativeAmericanHeritageMonth

text:
The biggest sex symbol of the ’90s Anna Nicole Smith is in absolutely unbelievable shape in this fucking video I just found - every curve on full display. Playboy’s Playmate of the Year, the face of Guess, and at 26 the bride of an 89-year-old oil billionaire who left her fighting for $88 million. Here she’s 34, about to let reality show cameras into her home 24 hours a day. The bathroom was the only place off-limits - until she forgot to switch off her microphone in there. The entire crew heard everything.

She never looked like the other models of her decade. While everyone else was rail-thin, she was soft, curvy and unapologetically glamorous - and the world couldn’t look away. In 1993 Playboy crowned her Playmate of the Year. Guess put her on billboards. A year later she married J. Howard Marshall II - 89 years old, worth a fortune. 14 months later he was gone, and she spent the next decade fighting his family for the money.

Then came the reality show.

E! offered her a show with cameras following her every second. She didn’t think twice. “I was like, okay, just go for it.” She didn’t ask about sleep, showers or privacy - she just said yes.

Seven weeks into filming, she sat down on a talk show to talk about it - and admitted the worst part.

The bathroom. The one room the cameras weren’t allowed into. One day she went in - and forgot her microphone was still on. The crew heard everything. “I was really embarrassed.”

The hosts couldn’t stop laughing. She laughed along.

The show premiered on August 4, 2002 - exactly 7 years to the day after her husband died - and pulled the highest cable ratings ever for a reality debut. That same year a judge awarded her $88 million from his estate.

But even that day, one detail stuck. Her son hated the cameras in their house. Four years later he was gone, just days after she welcomed her baby daughter - and five months after that, Anna Nicole Smith died at 39. Under that video today, the most-liked comments aren’t about her body or the scandals. They say she still seemed innocent and sweet. And that hopefully, she and Daniel are finally together, in peace.

Slim and famous or curvy and real - which Anna was hotter?
